ranked.question: Why do online early-exit rules stop so far short of the hindsight stop point: when an answer has formed, is whether it will later change already decided by the prefix (so a better signal can find it) or decided by later sampling (so no signal can)?

evidence.claim: The hindsight stop point is far earlier than any online rule reaches, and a simple agreement rule costs accuracy. Wrong traces also show an early fixed point.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Stopping each trace there would keep every answer at 0.35–0.44×the base model's tokens, but finding that point takes hindsight"; three agreeing forced answers cost 2.4-9.2 points; 59% of wrong traces also have an early fixed point

evidence.claim: The oracle for dynamic early exit needs a small fraction of the budget.
evidence.quote_or_number: oracle budget to match full thinking: dynamic early exit 14.2%, fixed budgets 35.0%, dynamic routing 71.4%

evidence.claim: About half of trajectories agree on an answer and later abandon it, and most of those still end correct.
evidence.quote_or_number: of 1,500 trajectories, 736 "agreed on an answer they went on to abandon"; 84.2% of those "still ended correct"; 155 of 216 non-terminal stops "commit a wrong answer to a trajectory that would have reached the right one"

evidence.claim: Real exit rules save a fifth to two fifths of tokens.
evidence.quote_or_number: "accuracy improvements of 0.9 to 4.8 points while reducing sequence length by 19.1% to 42.9%"

evidence.claim: Free continuations from a prefix carry more information than a forced answer, and using them as the exit signal multiplies total tokens.
evidence.quote_or_number: Qwen3-32B-Think at a 10% prefix: 70% recoverable, 34% correct under forced extraction; BAEE truncates 70-78% of serial generation, total tokens rise about 3-5x

evidence.claim: Single-pass probes for exit reach modest discrimination.
evidence.source: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right (arXiv 2504.05419); Token Budget Saturation (arXiv 2607.21433, abstract only)
evidence.quote_or_number: "ROC-AUC scores above 0.7"; 2607.21433 abstract: probe AUC 0.608

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly decided by the prefix: the per-prefix probability that the answer later changes is close to 0 or 1 for most prefixes, so the gap to the oracle is a matter of signal quality and signal cost.
ranked.why_uncertain: Half of trajectories abandon an agreed answer and most of them end correct anyway, which looks like sampling wandering between answers. Probe AUCs sit at 0.6-0.7 in several independent papers, which is what a ceiling set by sampling noise would produce. Sampling settings for these models are hot (temperature 0.6-1.0, presence penalty 1.5 in 2611.02278).
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: "early exit" AND reasoning AND (aleatoric OR irreducible OR branching OR resampling) AND answer -> 2608.27963 (SABER), 2610.25970 (GLOBE); "chain-of-thought" AND resampling AND counterfactual -> nothing (2506.19143 Thought Anchors checked by id); "post-commitment" -> 2604.06613, 2605.11467, 2605.11746; plus the termination and self-consensus papers already on the list (2610.13570, 2609.09989).
ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2609.09989 counts answers that are later abandoned and 2604.06613 uses fork agreement as a commitment definition, but neither splits the chance of a later change into a between-prefix part and a within-prefix sampling part. 2610.13570 computes the oracle, not why it is missed.
ranked.outcome_a: Prefix-decided: the oracle is reachable. Train a single-pass probe on fork outcomes (distil fork agreement into the hidden state) and run it in the engine; early exit can approach roughly 2x fewer thinking tokens.
ranked.outcome_b: Sampling-decided: the hindsight stop point is not a bound an online rule can reach, and exit gains cap near today's 20-40%. The tail then acts as a slow sequential resample of the answer; replace it with a few short forks at answer formation plus a vote (forks share the prefix KV), or remove it by training as Concise-9B does.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A fork-supervised exit probe, or fork-and-vote at answer formation in place of the tail.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-9B in vLLM with prefix caching, 200 problems, 2 base traces each. At the first fixed point (three consecutive agreeing forced readouts) and two later checkpoints, fork 16 free continuations and record each final answer. Measure the distribution of per-prefix flip probability p_i, the between-prefix share of flip variance 1 - E[p(1-p)] / (pbar(1-pbar)), and the AUC of a linear probe on the prefix hidden state against p_i. Stop if the between-prefix share is above 0.8 and existing trial-answer confidence already predicts flips with AUC above 0.9: then there is nothing left to explain.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: None with D1-D4. Outcome B's design touches the earlier Q03 (parallel versus sequential chains) but asks about forks at answer formation inside one request, not load crossover.

reasons.unpredictable: I have no basis to say whether the between-prefix share of flip variance is 0.3 or 0.8: probe AUCs of 0.6-0.7 fit either a weak signal or a sampling-noise ceiling, and hot sampling settings make both readings plausible. Experts in probing and in sampling would predict opposite answers.
reasons.generative: A gives a fork-supervised single-pass exit probe; B gives fork-and-vote at answer formation sharing prefix KV. Both outcomes name a distinct, buildable method and the variance decomposition chooses between them directly.
reasons.reviewer: Splitting the early-exit oracle gap into prefix-decided versus sampling-decided variance is a true missing limit; it would explain the 0.6-0.7 probe AUC plateau and either outcome gives a design (fork-distilled probe or fork-and-vote). Checked by arXiv query 2: related work (2604.06613, 2606.30852, 2606.13603) studies commitment and stopping rules, but no abstract shows this decomposition.
reasons.feasible: About 19k forked continuations with prefix caching in stock vLLM is under a GPU-day per 8-9B model. The variance decomposition and a linear probe on stored hidden states are simple analyses.

ranked.question: When sparse attention runs unverified and a reasoning model loses 16.5 points and runs 61% longer although roughly 95% of its tokens agree with dense, is the damage done by the few tokens that fall outside the dense model's nucleus, or by tokens that are individually plausible?

evidence.claim: Unverified sparse attention on reasoning: large accuracy loss that tracks cap-outs and length growth; per-step refresh still leaves +20% length.
evidence.quote_or_number: CVSA-c4 reaches 64.0% against dense 80.5% ... refreshing the selection every step (M=1) recovers two-thirds of the gap, to 75.0% ... cap-outs fall from 31 to 13 of 200 problems and generation-length inflation from +61% to +20% above dense. A residual 5.5-point gap remains

evidence.claim: Relaxed acceptance rules lengthen completions, and the extra tokens they admit have very low target probability.
evidence.quote_or_number: relaxed verification on average accepts 1.34× as many tokens per round but produces 1.54× longer completions ... The relaxed-only tokens are 7% to 24% of the committed draft tokens. For the four rules other than spec_casc_tok they have a median target probability of 0.01 to 0.09 (shared tokens: 0.78 to 0.93)

evidence.claim: With a truncated sampler, where out-of-support draft tokens are always rejected, the gentle rules stop inflating.
evidence.source: Acceptance Is Not Speed, arXiv 2610.23818 (section 3.3, Appendix C, Table A1 note)
evidence.quote_or_number: At Qwen3-8B’s recommended sampler (temperature 0.6), mentored_dec, cactus, and spec_casc_tok stop inflating on GSM8K and LiveCodeBench ... A draft token outside the target’s top-p/top-k support is rejected regardless of α.

evidence.claim: Lossless decoding at a slightly higher temperature also inflates length with accuracy unchanged, although every committed token is in the target's support.
evidence.source: Acceptance Is Not Speed, arXiv 2610.23818, Appendix C
evidence.quote_or_number: At T=1.2, GSM8K completions are 1.27× longer ([1.10,1.47]), rounds 1.37× and time 1.35×, with accuracy unchanged (0.96 against 0.97)

evidence.claim: Nucleus SD accepts every rejected draft token that lies in the target nucleus and reports accuracy slightly up, but measures speed as token throughput, not completion length.
evidence.source: Nucleus Speculative Decoding, arXiv 2610.07822 (abstract, setup, results)
evidence.quote_or_number: over half of the rejected tokens lie inside the target’s own nucleus ... NSD’s accuracy difference relative to SD ranges from −1.58 to +4.14 percentage points, with NSD achieving 0.40 percentage points higher accuracy on average ... Speedup Ratio is the ratio of each method’s token throughput to target model autoregressive (AR) throughput

evidence.claim: The drafter matters for inflation: real language-model drafters inflate least. A sparse self-draft is the strongest such drafter and was not tested.
evidence.quote_or_number: Its median varies more with the rule (0.97 for spec_casc_tok to 1.39 for cactus) and the drafter (0.94 for standalone drafters to 1.23 for EAGLE heads) than with the task

evidence.claim: Weight quantization and KV eviction also lengthen reasoning, sometimes with accuracy kept.
evidence.source: Quantization Inflates Reasoning, arXiv 2606.25519 (abstract); Hold Onto That Thought, arXiv 2512.12008 (abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: INT4/INT3 quantization can preserve accuracy but increase reasoning-token usage ... eviction strategies at low budgets can produce longer reasoning traces

ranked.expert_prediction: Out-of-nucleus tokens do most of the damage. A sparse self-draft checked only by 'is the draft token inside the dense nucleus' would keep length and accuracy close to dense.
ranked.why_uncertain: Three results point the other way. Lossless sampling at T=1.2 lengthens GSM8K by 1.27x with accuracy unchanged, and there every token is in-support, only less likely. CVSA with per-step refresh, where the output error is bounded by the coverage identity, still runs 20% longer. And sparse-attention error is systematic rather than random: the same missing context biases the same decision again and again (for example whether an intermediate result was already derived), and a 're-check' token is individually plausible. Nucleus SD's accuracy claim does not settle it because it reports tokens per second, the metric Acceptance Is Not Speed shows is blind to length.

ranked.question: When sparse-attention (or low-bit) decoding makes a reasoning model run long and fail to finish, does the damage enter through the few tokens a full pass would have rejected, or through the KV entries that were written under the approximation?

evidence.claim: ReSA attributes sparse-decoding loss to the KV cache, repairs only the KV (tokens are kept, never checked) and recovers almost all accuracy; it never separates KV error from wrong tokens.
evidence.source: Rectified Sparse Attention, arXiv 2506.04108 (Abstract, Sec 2.2, App B, Table 1)
evidence.quote_or_number: "suffer from KV cache misalignment, where approximation errors accumulate and degrade generation quality"; "ReSA does not rely on output logits to make per-token accept / reject decisions"; math 7B: Dense 60.72, Sparse 57.72, ReSA 60.52

evidence.claim: SparseSpec repairs tokens (lossless verification) and gets about 94% per-token acceptance from a 5% KV budget on Qwen3 reasoning.
evidence.quote_or_number: "PillarAttn achieves an average acceptance token length of 6.16 out of 8 tokens"; "We set the sparsity ratio to 0.05"

evidence.claim: With no repair of either kind, sparse decoding at a similar budget on the same model family loses 15 to 20 points, almost all by not finishing.
evidence.quote_or_number: Qwen3-4B full 48.3% vs ours@512 33.3%; "Most of the loss is truncation at 16K (Quest@512 70% vs full 41%); accuracy on finished samples is 73-80% for every non-SnapKV run."

evidence.claim: For low-bit weights on agent tasks, the state channel is measurable and large: keeping low-precision KV costs success, and a 3-bit decoder reading a top-tier prefill recovers most of it.
evidence.source: Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing, arXiv 2602.02711 (App F, Sec 3.2)
evidence.quote_or_number: "decreasing task success by 6.6 percentage points (68.2% to 61.6%)"; success "increases from 29.6% to 79.2% on ALFWorld"

evidence.claim: For quantized reasoning models the published account is token-level: divergence concentrates at high-entropy positions where overthinking markers get sampled.
evidence.source: Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not, arXiv 2606.00206 (Abstract, Sec 4.3)
evidence.quote_or_number: "in up to 52% of the quantized models' failures, models reach the right answer in intermediate reasoning steps but do not output it as a final answer"; Spearman rho = 0.92 between position-level KL and full-precision entropy

evidence.claim: In the user's SubSpec work a 4-bit draft loses 17-38% of its acceptance length when it reads KV it wrote itself instead of KV written by the fp16 target; the cause was never confirmed.
evidence.quote_or_number: "systematically 17-38% lower acceptance than SubSpec at identical d/K/temperature configs"; d=32 K=6: 18.4 vs 12.2

evidence.claim: The lossy speculative decoding study states that the mechanism from a committed unlikely token to longer thinking is not shown.
evidence.quote_or_number: "They do not show why an unlikely token makes a reasoning model think more rather than less."

ranked.expert_prediction: Both channels matter. At mild sparsity (ReSA's regime) rewriting the KV recovers most of the loss; at a 4-5% budget wrong tokens dominate, so KV rewrite alone recovers well under half.
ranked.why_uncertain: The two published repairs point in opposite directions and neither ran the control. ReSA's rectification also refreshes the block selection, so its gain may not be a KV effect at all. DMR shows a large state effect for low-bit weights, while 2606.00206 describes the same family of failures as token-level. The user's own 17-38% acceptance gap from draft-written KV is bigger than SubSpec's published KV-sharing ablation (tau 23.07 to 25.14) and was never confirmed.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arxiv.org listings: 'speculative decoding rejected tokens reasoning', 'self-speculative decoding draft', 'sparse attention reasoning'; WebSearch: 'which tokens rejected sparse attention draft self-speculative decoding ... lossy sparse decoding derail critical tokens 2026'. Closest found: ReSA 2506.04108 Appendix B, which compares against sparse self-speculation on speed only, with no accuracy or acceptance numbers.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: ReSA (2506.04108) for sparse attention and DMR Appendix F (2602.02711) for low-bit weights at agent-step granularity. Neither separates the two channels on long reasoning traces; ASPIRE (2609.17943) does not say whether draft-written KV is overwritten and does not analyse which tokens are rejected.
ranked.outcome_a: State channel dominates: tokens produced under sparse attention are fine, the stored KV is what rots. Build sparse (or 4-bit) decoding with a periodic batched dense rewrite of the recent KV and no token verification. That removes the rollback and the acceptance bookkeeping from SparseSpec-style systems and makes the dense pass a pure prefill-shaped batch.
ranked.outcome_b: Token channel dominates: a small set of committed tokens derails the trace. Build verify-on-demand: sparse decoding plus a cheap detector for the positions a full pass would reject, with full attention only there; lossless speculative decoding can then skip rewriting draft KV for accepted tokens.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a KV-rewrite-only fast path (no token verification) or a token-verify-only fast path (no KV rewrite) for sparse and low-bit decoding of long reasoning traces.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-4B, AIME 30 problems x 8 samples, kv-fetch selector at budget 512, 16K cap. 2x2 arms: tokens {as produced by sparse attention; replaced by the full-attention choice under the same sampling noise} x KV {sparse-written; rewritten by a dense pass every 32 tokens}. Add one pair with 4-bit weights in place of sparse attention to test the same split for quantization and to settle the subspec_v2 gap. Measure cap-hit rate, mean length, accuracy. First, for free, check on stored outputs whether capped samples already contain the correct answer. Stop if neither single repair recovers more than a third of the gap to full attention (the channels then interact and no cheap single fix exists).
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Builds on the D1 residue (lossy page selection fails by not finishing) but is not a selector question. Near residue (a); differs by asking where the error enters, tested by intervention.

reasons.unpredictable: I lean toward the token channel dominating at a 4-5% budget, but the user's own 17-38% acceptance gap from draft-written KV and ReSA's result point to the state channel, and neither published repair ran the control. I could not predict which single repair recovers more.
reasons.generative: A gives a KV-rewrite-only fast path with no token verification or rollback; B gives a verify-on-demand path with no KV rewrite. Either outcome restructures SparseSpec-style systems, and the 2x2 intervention maps directly onto the two architectures.
reasons.reviewer: The 2x2 of token channel versus approximation-written KV is an intervention neither ReSA nor DMR ran, and the two outcomes give opposite fast paths (KV rewrite without verification, or verification without rewrite). 'Both channels interact' is a plausible flat result.
reasons.feasible: The 2x2 needs a custom closed-loop engine that runs sparse and dense passes per step, swaps tokens under shared sampling noise and rewrites KV every 32 tokens, on 16K-cap traces. 30 AIME problems x 8 samples gives coarse cap-hit statistics, so plan two to three weeks.

ranked.question: When a relaxed (lossy) verification rule makes a reasoning model's completion longer, is the length change a function of one number (how much the admitted tokens raise realized surprisal under the target, an effective temperature) or does it depend on where and what the admitted tokens are (decisions to close the thinking block, overthinking marker words, drafter type)?

evidence.claim: Relaxed verification accepts more per round but lengthens completions by more than it saves.
evidence.quote_or_number: "relaxed verification on average accepts 1.34× as many tokens per round but produces 1.54× longer completions"

evidence.claim: Inflation varies more with the rule and the drafter type than with the task.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Its median varies more with the rule (0.97 for spec_casc_tok to 1.39 for cactus) and the drafter (0.94 for standalone drafters to 1.23 for EAGLE heads) than with the task (1.04 on GSM8K to 1.14 on HumanEval)"

evidence.claim: A temperature control reproduces inflation on one model but not the other, which still inflates under relaxed rules.
evidence.quote_or_number: "raising the sampling temperature from 1.0 to 1.2 ... lengthens GPT-OSS-20B completions by 1.27× on GSM8K" versus "Qwen3-8B behaves differently: its completions barely lengthen at T=1.2 or 1.5 (λ 1.02 to 1.04 ...)"; "spec_casc_opt still inflates by 1.5×" at Qwen3-8B's recommended temperature 0.6

evidence.claim: The authors state the mechanism is open.
evidence.quote_or_number: "They do not show why an unlikely token makes a reasoning model think more rather than less."

evidence.claim: Most extra tokens come after the correct answer already appeared, and a per-token guard does not generalise.
evidence.quote_or_number: "On GSM8K, 50% (GPT-OSS-20B) and 82% (Qwen3-8B) of the extra tokens come after it"; guard "cut the eight cases from 13 364 to 10 534 tokens ...; on all 30 cases it moved the mean from 9 270 to 10 363 tokens"

evidence.claim: A competing lossy rule admits only high-rank tokens and reports throughput per token, so completion length is not in its metric.
evidence.quote_or_number: "The tokens rescued by NSD are highly plausible under the target: 94.1% rank within its top five"; "Speedup Ratio is the ratio of each method's token throughput to target model autoregressive (AR) throughput"

evidence.claim: For weight quantization, lengthening is tied to a token class at high-entropy positions, not to a global dose.
evidence.quote_or_number: "at these positions quantized models disproportionately sample overthinking markers such as \"wait\", \"but\", and \"alternatively\""

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly a dose effect: admissions inside the target's nucleus (rank 1-5) are harmless, low-probability admissions (rank 37-234) push the trace off-distribution like a higher temperature would, and inflation grows with the mean surprisal of admitted tokens. Position and token class are second-order.
ranked.why_uncertain: Three numbers in the one paper that measured it do not fit a pure dose story: Qwen3-8B barely lengthens when temperature is raised to 1.5 yet inflates under relaxed rules; the drafter type (standalone 0.94 versus EAGLE head 1.23) moves the median more than the task does; and 82% of extra tokens come after the answer is already written, which points to a failure to stop rather than to more reasoning. The quantization literature found a token-class mechanism instead of a dose. Nobody has intervened on token rank, position and class separately.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API queries: "length inflation" AND speculative; "speculative decoding" AND (lossy OR relaxed) AND reasoning; reasoning length AND (perturbation OR injection OR intervention); termination OR "</think>" AND reasoning model; grep of 2610.23818 for markers, hazard and 2606.00206 (none). Closest: 2610.23818 (documents the effect, states it does not explain it). No token-injection dose-response study found for 2025-2026.

ranked.outcome_b: If position or class dominates (for example overrides near the close-of-thinking decision or marker words account for most of the inflation at equal surprisal): one builds a verifier that is strict only at those positions and loose elsewhere, and the per-token guard in 2610.23818 fails for an identifiable reason (it cannot see trace state).
ranked.design_it_points_to: A relaxed verification rule for reasoning models with a predictable length cost: either a surprisal budget (A) or a trace-state-aware gate around termination and marker tokens (B).

ranked.question: Is the plateau that six retrained drafter recipes converge to the target model's own ceiling for deterministic drafts at temperature 1, or a training limit the recipes share, i.e. what share of rejections happen where the target itself is near-tied versus where the target is confident and the drafter is wrong?
ranked.tension_type: missing limit (with a contradiction inside one paper)

evidence.claim: The only bound paper says both that there is large room and that algorithms approach the limit.
evidence.quote_or_number: "about ×2 difference between the theoretical bound and EAGLE-3 is caused by a speculation error. This suggests that there is still significant room for improvement" and "This suggests that current deterministic algorithms are approaching the fundamental limits under the assumptions studied"

evidence.claim: The bound rests on an i.i.d. assumption the authors say is not exact, and excludes sampled drafts.
evidence.quote_or_number: "The analysis depends on Assumption 2, which states that the distributions of acceptance probabilities are independent and identically distributed across prefixes. This is not exact for language models"

evidence.claim: Under one training protocol, six drafter recipes converge.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the maximum-minus-minimum speedup gap falls from 1.36 in published results to 0.85 after remeasurement and 0.23 after retraining"; Table 1 Qwen3-8B budget 16, 1|0, high-entropy accepted length 3.19 (DFlash) to 3.56 (Domino)

evidence.claim: Standard drafter training has stopped improving.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Baseline +1 epoch yields minimal macro-average changes (Δ≤0.03 tokens) across all configurations, indicating that standard token-level training has largely plateaued"

evidence.claim: Targets whose entropy statistic differs 4.5 times get nearly the same accepted length from EAGLE-3.
evidence.quote_or_number: mean μ 0.683 (Llama-3 8B) versus 0.153 (Llama-3 70B) at T=1; EAGLE-3 mean accepted length at T=1: 4.92 (8B) versus 5.66 (70B)

evidence.claim: The tree ceiling in the literature is conditional on the tree the drafter built, not on what the target allows.
evidence.quote_or_number: "one plus target coverage sharply bounds the expected output-block length, including the bonus token, of any exact path verifier"

evidence.claim: The vLLM study's upper bound is a different object: it removes wasted verification, it does not bound accepted length.
evidence.quote_or_number: "The oracle speedup represents an upper bound in which the accepted length at each decoding step is known in advance, and the system proposes exactly that many tokens."

ranked.expert_prediction: Drafters use roughly 50-70% of the exact ceiling on high-entropy text with 8B targets, more on chat, and much less on large or low-entropy targets where the target is confident and the small drafter is simply wrong.
ranked.why_uncertain: The exact per-context ceiling has not been computed for any current drafter. With a deterministic draft at T=1 a token is accepted with probability equal to the target's probability of it, so the best chain is the target's most probable continuation and the best N-node tree is its N most probable prefixes; both are computable from the target alone without the i.i.d. assumption. The convergence of six recipes and the training plateau fit a ceiling; the near-equal accepted length across targets with a 4.5 times entropy difference fits a drafter-side limit. The one theory paper draws both conclusions.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API queries: speculative decoding AND (ceiling OR headroom OR "fundamental limit"); AND oracle; AND "target entropy"; optimal draft tree; "upper bound" AND oracle. Semantic Scholar citations of 2512.11718 (one citing survey). One web search on oracle upper bound versus trained drafters. Read section 8 of 2601.11580 to check its bound.

ranked.outcome_a: If drafters already use most of the ceiling (above about 85%) on the text measured: further deterministic-drafter training is wasted there, and the work moves to sampled or coupled drafts (the 1|1 numbers 4.09-4.18 already exceed the 1|0 ones), target-shaped trees, or lossy rules.
ranked.outcome_b: If drafters are far below the ceiling: the six recipes share a training limit. The rejection labels say which positions carry the loss (target confident, drafter wrong), and one builds a loss or data selection aimed at those positions, with the largest payoff on large low-entropy targets.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a stop sign for drafter training with a pointer to stochastic drafting (A), or a position-targeted drafter objective with a measured headroom number (B). In both cases a reusable per-context ceiling tool for any target.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B (thinking off first) with released DFlash, DSpark and EAGLE-3 checkpoints; MT-Bench and GSM8K; target T=1, greedy draft. Also compare the sampled-draft (1|1) accepted length with the deterministic ceiling. Report the ceiling-use ratio per task and drafter. Stop signal: if the ratio is above 0.85 everywhere, the question is answered as A; if it is below 0.5 with most rejections at confident positions, it is answered as B.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: none. Not a profiling exercise (D3): it measures a model-side limit, not a system bottleneck.

Slight lean toward 'closer to the ceiling than people think' on chat text, but weak.

Reviewers will note the ceiling only binds deterministic drafts at T=1.

ranked.question: What sets how long a reasoning model keeps thinking after its answer has formed: a length budget fixed at the prompt that the tail fills, or a verification pass whose length scales with the derivation?

evidence.claim: Total thinking length is largely fixed from the question before any reasoning is generated.
evidence.source: On Reasoning Strength Planning in Large Reasoning Models (arXiv 2506.08390)
evidence.quote_or_number: "a correlation of 0.84 between predicted and actual values"

evidence.claim: The redundant share varies widely across samples of the same question, and by model, with no explanation offered.
evidence.quote_or_number: overthinking ratio 41.1% (GPT-OSS-20B) to 74.4% (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking); within-question mean pairwise absolute difference 20.23 pp; "Greater length redundancy does not imply greater accuracy degradation."

evidence.claim: Training can halve the post-answer part while barely changing the pre-answer part, and one model family has almost no removable tail.
evidence.quote_or_number: post-answer thinking 7,506 -> 3,692 tokens, pre-answer 5,137 -> 4,538; Olmo-3-7B-Think saves only 1-4%

evidence.claim: The point where the answer stabilises differs several-fold between model families.
evidence.quote_or_number: gemma-4-26B-A4B-it reaches its final answer after 13-23% of CoT tokens; gpt-oss-20b after 43-68%

evidence.claim: Thinking mode raises the post-commitment share relative to no-think mode of the same weights.
evidence.quote_or_number: MATH-500: Qwen3-32B-Think 75% vs NoThink 61%; Qwen3-8B-Think 73% vs NoThink 52%

evidence.claim: The halt direction's cut tracks each problem's slack, and the base model runs about twice past saturation.
evidence.quote_or_number: saturation about 1,650 think tokens vs median about 3,700 (factor 2.24); "the cut tracks each problem's own removable slack at 0.70"

ranked.expert_prediction: Within a question, samples that take longer to reach the answer also have longer tails (positive correlation): checks scale with what there is to check, and training sets the ratio.
ranked.why_uncertain: If total length is planned from the question (r = 0.84), a sample that reaches the answer late has less budget left and the tail should be shorter: a negative within-question correlation. The two readings predict opposite signs and no paper reports the within-question covariance. The Concise-9B result (tail halves, derivation barely moves) fits a separable habit better than proportional checking.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: "reasoning length" AND "within-problem" -> nothing; thinking tokens AND variance AND "same prompt" -> nothing; thinking tokens AND ("verification phase" OR "self-verification") AND length AND (proportional OR budget) -> nothing; "post-commitment" -> 2604.06613, 2605.11467, 2605.11746; overthinking and termination topic queries -> 2610.13570, 2605.27965, 2606.02835.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2610.13570 reports the within-question spread of the redundant share (20.23 pp) and 2611.02278 reports pre- and post-answer token counts, but neither relates time-to-answer to tail length within a question or tests the budget-fill reading from 2506.08390.
ranked.outcome_a: Budget-fill (negative within-question correlation; total length fixed by the prompt): length is a plan made at the prompt. Build a one-shot prompt-time correction (lower the planned strength by the predicted slack, or train the plan) with no online monitor; prompt-level length predictors are enough for scheduling; lossy-method inflation is then a shift of the plan (links to card 1).
ranked.outcome_b: Proportional verification (positive correlation): the tail is a re-read of the derivation and costs in proportion to it. Build exit at answer formation, or make the check cheap (longer drafts, sparse attention, a smaller verifier); it also says the tail is where old KV is read (links to card 2).
ranked.design_it_points_to: Prompt-time length correction with no monitor, or a cheap verification path for the tail.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B and gpt-oss-20b in vLLM; 150 problems (MATH-500 level 5, AIME 2024/2025), 16 samples each at the recommended sampling settings, 32K cap. Close thinking every 512 tokens through prefix-cached forks to find when the answer forms (t_c); tail = length - t_c. Report the within-problem correlation of t_c and tail with problem fixed effects, the between-problem correlation, and the share of total-length variance explained by problem identity, per model family. Stop if the within-problem correlation is inside +/-0.1 for all three models, or if t_c moves materially between 256- and 512-token readout intervals (measurement too coarse to carry a design).
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near the earlier Q12 (how much of length is fixed by the prompt, for schedulers). It differs by splitting length at answer formation and asking for the mechanism of the tail. None of D1-D4.

reasons.unpredictable: The two published readings predict opposite signs for the within-question correlation; I lean weakly positive because sample-level verbosity is a common factor for both segments, but a near-zero result is just as likely. Nobody has reported this covariance.
reasons.generative: A gives a prompt-time length correction with no online monitor, a real design; B's 'make the check cheap' is vague and mostly defers to exit-at-commit from other cards.
reasons.reviewer: Opposite-sign predictions for the within-question correlation make a neat test (query 2 found no paper reporting it). The evidence is correlational and the prompt-time correction design is vague.

ranked.question: A sparse-KV self-draft whose selection is fresh is still rejected on about 5% of tokens: are those the tokens where the dense target is itself close to undecided (so any small perturbation loses them), or tokens where one needed KV entry was missing and the draft is confidently wrong?

evidence.claim: With zero staleness a 7% sparse draft is accepted about 95% of the time, and with per-step refresh the decay with draft length is what a constant 5% per-token loss gives (0.95(1-0.95^10)/(0.05*10)=0.762, my arithmetic, assuming acceptance = accepted/drafted).
evidence.quote_or_number: At γ=1 both variants achieve near-identical acceptance (∼95%), since the context has not yet gone stale. As draft length grows, the gap widens steadily: without refresh, acceptance drops to 60.3% at γ=10, whereas with refresh it remains at 76.6%, a 16.4 pp gap.

evidence.claim: A different system at 5% budget and temperature 1.0 gets the same first-position number, and the loss is not a fixed floor: ten times the budget removes most of it.
evidence.source: S3R, arXiv 2610.13202 (body, Appendix E.2 and budget sweep)
evidence.quote_or_number: acceptance falls from 95.8% for the first proposed token to 67.9% for the sixth ... Increasing s from 0.05 to 0.50 raises acceptance from 80.4% to 96.7%, while speedup falls from 1.370× to 1.058×.

evidence.claim: SparseSpec reports the opposite about budget: more selected tokens stop helping at 5%. 6.16 of 8 accepted corresponds to an iid per-token rate of about 0.94 (my arithmetic).
evidence.quote_or_number: PillarAttn achieves an average acceptance token length of 6.16 out of 8 tokens ... We set the sparsity ratio to 0.05, as performance saturates with further increases in selected tokens.

evidence.claim: Acceptance of a sparse-KV self-draft barely changes between greedy and hot sampling, while a small-model draft falls from 0.4649 to 0.2664 over the same range.
For a quantized self-draft, agreement tracks target entropy almost perfectly in aggregate (across RL training steps, not per token).
evidence.quote_or_number: target-output entropy and token-level agreement between ℳp and its weight-quantized copy Q(ℳp) show a strong negative correlation (r=−0.99)

evidence.claim: Per token, the sparse draft's own entropy predicts acceptance poorly.
evidence.quote_or_number: negative draft entropy obtains an acceptance AUC of 0.638 on RULER QA1. Tokens in the low-entropy bin are accepted at 86.3%, compared with 62.1% in the high-entropy bin.

evidence.claim: Most target positions are sharply peaked, so under greedy decoding only a minority of positions can flip from small noise.
evidence.source: When Is a Draft Accepted?, arXiv 2606.30265 (body)
evidence.quote_or_number: the mean top token probability is ≈0.85 for Qwen3-1.7B and ≈0.87 for Qwen3-4B, and the median is even higher at ≈0.97 and ≈0.99

evidence.claim: Coverage failures of sparse attention are intermittent and move between heads from step to step.
evidence.quote_or_number: intermittent cells failing on 5–80% of steps account for 86.4%, and the set of failing heads overlaps by a Jaccard index of only 0.33 between consecutive steps

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly the target: rejections sit at low-margin, high-entropy positions, the selector matters little once coverage is high, and a small tail is true retrieval misses.
ranked.why_uncertain: If rejections were small noise acting at low-margin positions, greedy acceptance (only argmax flips count) should be well above sampling acceptance (1 - TV, which collects loss at every position), because the median top-token probability is 0.97-0.99. TriForce's table shows 0.9234 at T=0 against 0.9004 at T=1.0, almost the same, which fits a fixed subset of positions where the draft is grossly off. S3R's sweep (80.4% to 96.7% from 5% to 50% budget) says the loss is not draft-independent, while SparseSpec says it saturates at 5%. The draft's own entropy has AUC 0.638, so the draft often does not know. Against that, the r=-0.99 entropy correlation for a quantized draft says the target decides.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: 'speculative decoding' + sparse + entropy + acceptance (no hits); 'self-speculative' + acceptance + (margin OR coverage) (only SparseSpec-L); 'speculative decoding' + acceptance + ('target entropy' OR 'predict acceptance') (SpecDec++ 2405.19715); 'speculative decoding' + 'rejected tokens' (Nucleus SD, Oilbird, none on sparse self-drafts); 'speculative decoding' + ('sparse attention' OR 'sparse KV') (20 hits, all checked). WebSearch: per-token rejection of sparse self-drafts against target entropy and attention coverage (no direct paper).
ranked.closest_existing_answer: SparseSpec-L (2607.27735) bins acceptance by draft entropy on one task and says entropy is not a calibrated predictor. CVSA (2611.10634) ties coverage exactly to attention-output error but never to token acceptance. 'When Is a Draft Accepted?' (2606.30265) gives margin theory for general drafts with no self-speculation experiment. None decomposes sparse-draft rejections by cause.
ranked.outcome_a: Target-determined: rejection is predicted by target entropy or margin and coverage adds almost nothing. Then better selectors (PillarAttn, Vegas, refresh layers) have little headroom left; use the cheapest engine-friendly selection (page-granular), set draft length from recent target entropy, and look for speed in making the draft cheaper rather than more accurate.
ranked.outcome_b: Miss-determined: rejection is predicted by per-head coverage drops and the draft is confident when wrong. Then the draft cannot stop itself by its own entropy; build a coverage-triggered early verify (CVSA's check as the draft-length controller) and give the intermittent failing heads extra budget.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either an entropy-driven draft-length controller on top of a deliberately crude selector (A), or a coverage-triggered verification trigger with per-head budgets (B). It also tells whether the user's SparseSpec line should invest in selection at all.
ranked.first_experiment: Offline, no serving engine. Qwen3-8B (dense attention), about 200 reasoning traces from AIME / LiveCodeBench / MATH-500, 4-8K generated tokens each, replayed teacher-forced. Two-stream forward in PyTorch: dense stream gives K/V and the target distribution p at every position; a sparse query stream attends to top-K entries of the dense K/V. Selection variants: oracle top-K from the token's own dense attention, and previous-step top-K (zero staleness, PillarAttn-style). Budgets 2, 5, 10, 25, 50%. Log per position: TV(p,q), argmax agreement, target entropy, top-2 margin, draft entropy, per-layer and per-head coverage. Analyse: AUC of rejection from target-only features, coverage-only features, and both; share of total TV carried by the worst 5% of positions; overlap of the greedy and T=1 rejection sets. Decide A if target-only AUC >= 0.85 and coverage adds < 0.02; decide B if coverage adds >= 0.10 or oracle selection halves rejection at equal budget. Stop if neither feature family reaches AUC 0.7: the instrument is wrong.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near D1 (decode-time KV page selection) only in subject. D1 asked whether fetching selected pages saves time in the engine; this asks what limits acceptance, measured offline, and outcome A would say selection quality is not the lever. Not Q01, Q02 or Q22 (no load or cost-ratio condition).

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict a mixed result: target margin predicts most rejections (AUC about 0.75-0.8) with a confident-wrong retrieval-miss tail that coverage explains partly, landing between the card's thresholds. The near-equal T=0/T=1 acceptance is a real puzzle, so not fully predictable.
reasons.generative: A gives an entropy-driven draft-length controller over a deliberately crude page-granular selector; B gives a coverage-triggered early verify with per-head budgets. Both are buildable in the user's SparseSpec line, though A partly amounts to 'stop investing in selection'.
reasons.reviewer: Decomposing sparse self-draft rejections into target-undecided versus missing-entry is unmeasured and grounded in a real anomaly (TriForce T=0 vs T=1). It decides between two controller designs and whether selector quality has headroom, though the audience for sparse self-speculation is narrow.
reasons.feasible: Offline teacher-forced replay on an 8B model fits one card and the AUC analysis is simple. The two-stream forward (sparse queries over dense K/V with per-head top-K masks on 4-8K traces) is a few days of custom attention code before any number appears.

ranked.question: When a lossy method (weight quantization, KV quantization, KV eviction or sparse attention, bf16 state rounding) makes a reasoning model think longer, is the cause the persistent, systematic same-direction part of the error (removable by unbiased/stochastic rounding, a bias correction, or randomising the error at equal size) or the per-step size of the error whatever its direction?

evidence.claim: For recurrent-state rounding in hybrids, an unbiased rounding rule at the same width removes the length increase, so the authors attribute it to bias. Weight quantization was not tested.
evidence.source: arXiv 2611.12127, Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of the five affected models."; "so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution."

evidence.claim: For weight quantization the published explanation is noise acting at uncertain positions. There is no random-noise or unbiased-rounding control, and round-to-nearest was not tested.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Position-level KL divergence correlates strongly with the BF16 model's next-token entropy (Spearman ρ=0.92)."; the margin argument "provides intuition for one specific failure mode, not a complete causal explanation"

evidence.claim: At the same bit width and group size, plain round-to-nearest inflates length about seven to ten times more than a data-free quantizer that optimises scale and zero point, and the average is never negative for any configuration.
evidence.source: arXiv 2606.25519, Quantization Inflates Reasoning: Token Inflation as a Hidden Cost (full text, Table 2)
evidence.quote_or_number: Average CTIR at INT4: Qwen3-4B RTN +42.5%, HQQ +6.0%, GPTQ +12.0%, AWQ +8.2%; Qwen3-30B RTN +43.0%, HQQ +3.9%, GPTQ +3.7%, AWQ +14.4%.

evidence.claim: An earlier systematic study reported no length increase at all, so the effect depends on something about the quantizer that has not been identified.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Contrary to expectations, quantized models do not exhibit increased output lengths."

evidence.claim: Two different 4-bit checkpoints of the same model differ in outcomes about as much as 4-bit differs from full precision, so any length comparison needs a noise floor from a perturbation that should not matter.
evidence.source: arXiv 2610.24346, Measuring the Task Value of Precision Upgrades in Closed-Loop Agents (abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: "replacing an action with that of a second 4-bit checkpoint changed about as many outcomes as replacing it with the BF16 action"

evidence.claim: The quantization paper explains longer thinking as noise that tips sampling toward continuation markers at uncertain positions, and never measures the stop decision.
evidence.source: Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not (arXiv 2606.00206)
evidence.quote_or_number: "quantization noise can shift the sampled token toward an overthinking marker such as "Wait" or "But""; position-level KL vs full-precision next-token entropy Spearman 0.92; marker penalty cuts CoT length 12-23%

evidence.claim: For bf16 recurrent state in hybrid models, rounding with the same width but no bias removes the lengthening, so error size alone is not the cause there. The offline quantity it tried (teacher-forced KL per head group) ranked head groups wrongly.
evidence.source: Lost in Rounding: bf16 Recurrent State Makes Hybrid Reasoning Models Think Longer (arXiv 2611.12127)
evidence.quote_or_number: length x1.07 to x1.27 on five of six models; Qwen3.5-9B accuracy 85.6% -> 70.8% under bf16, 87.6% with stochastic rounding; length increase removed in four of five affected models; head octile with 49% of the KL had no length effect

evidence.claim: One direction in activation space controls thinking length, but a push in a random direction also lengthens generation. The paper has no test under quantization or KV compression.
evidence.quote_or_number: steering strength vs length rho = -0.82; random direction about 10% longer; "Satisfying a single scalar leaves the off-axis dimensions unconstrained, and they move"

evidence.claim: Thinking length is planned before generation and readable by a linear probe; the end-of-thinking logit follows the plan.
evidence.source: On Reasoning Strength Planning in Large Reasoning Models (arXiv 2506.08390)
evidence.quote_or_number: "a correlation of 0.84 between predicted and actual values"; "the changes in the logits of the end-of-reasoning token are the result of planning, rather than the cause of planning."

evidence.claim: Length-steering directions survive weight quantization almost unchanged, but the paper does not measure whether quantization moves the state along them, uses no reasoning models and no KV methods.
evidence.quote_or_number: "cosine similarity 0.989-0.998 for INT8, 0.945-0.990 for NF4"; applying the FP16 vector to quantized models "is deferred to follow-up work"

evidence.claim: KV eviction lengthens thinking on most problems and the paper offers no mechanism.
evidence.quote_or_number: R-KV at 25% on MATH-500: 3,268.7 -> 4,538.1 tokens (+38.8%) on R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, +79.0% on R1-Distill-Llama-8B; 399 of 500 problems longer

evidence.claim: Lossy speculative decoding, a one-sided perturbation toward the draft, also lengthens reasoning (abstract only).
evidence.quote_or_number: "on average accepts $1.34\times$ as many tokens per round but produces $1.54\times$ longer completions"

evidence.claim: For hybrid recurrent state, the same bit width with stochastic rounding removes most of the length increase; the paper says the cause is bias, not resolution, and that the highest teacher-forced-KL parts do not localise it.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution"; Qwen3.5-9B: "cap hits rise from 118 to 223 and accuracy falls from 85.6% to 70.8%"

evidence.claim: For KV eviction at a matched budget, replacing deterministic top-k with sampling raises accuracy; the stated reason (diversity) is not measured.
evidence.quote_or_number: SnapKV 64.3% to 70.9% and CurDKV 78.6% to 87.6% (GSM8K, Qwen3-4B, K=512); "We attribute this to improved diversity of the retained KV pairs"

evidence.claim: In the user's runs the set that minimises missing attention at every step is not the most accurate one.
evidence.quote_or_number: "oracle@1024 39.2%: ours@1024 is +2.1 points above it [-0.8, +5.0] (minimum missing attention per step is not maximum accuracy)"

evidence.claim: Per-step KL does not rank the user's two models: the hybrid has about 3x lower next-token KL at budget 512 but loses at least as many points online.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Qwen3.5's oracle@512 gives next-token KL 0.011 at 22.9% missing; Qwen3-4B 0.035 at 14.1%"; online at 512: Qwen3.5 49.6% to 30.0%, Qwen3-4B 48.3% to 33.3%

evidence.claim: Against: unbiased token-level noise (higher temperature, lossless) also lengthens reasoning.
evidence.quote_or_number: temperature 1.2 lengthens GPT-OSS-20B completions 1.27x on GSM8K

evidence.claim: Against: one line of work holds that recall is the lever and a single miss is enough.
evidence.quote_or_number: "missing even one critical key can lead to sharp error spikes"

evidence.claim: The sparse-attention length study explains inflation as lost information that the model rebuilds, but never measures the loss per step.
evidence.quote_or_number: "consistently increase output length by up to 90% on reasoning-intensive datasets"; "the model repeats content when trying to rebuild context"

ranked.expert_prediction: Size. Inflation tracks output divergence (total variation), so stochastic rounding, which has about twice the rounding variance of round-to-nearest, would inflate length more, not less; the gap between RTN and HQQ or GPTQ is just a gap in output error.
ranked.why_uncertain: The only experiment that separates the two readings (2611.12127) came out the other way, though for state, where the same rounding repeats every step. For weights the error is fixed, so the analogue of bias is a consistent shift of each layer's output mean. Two things fit that reading better than the size reading: the average length change is positive in every published configuration (a zero-mean disturbance should sometimes shorten), and a data-free quantizer cuts inflation from +42.5% to +6.0% at the same bit width.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: "weight quantization reasoning length inflation stochastic rounding OR Gaussian noise control matched perturbation chain-of-thought tokens longer quantized LLM 2026" (no such control found). Semantic Scholar citations of 2606.00206 (seventeen), 2606.25519 (two) and 2611.12127 (none). Read 2606.00206, 2606.25519 and 2611.12127 in full looking for a noise or unbiased-rounding control on weights: none.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: arXiv 2611.12127 (the same test, but on recurrent state, not weights). For weights, arXiv 2610.00694 includes isotropic Gaussian weight noise but only measures teacher-forced flips, not generation length.
ranked.outcome_a: Systematic part: stochastic rounding or a per-channel bias correction removes most of the inflation at the same width even though the squared error is equal or larger. Then the fix is cheap and data-free, quantizers should be scored by mean shift (for example at the end-of-thinking and hesitation-marker logits) and not by squared error, and plain RTN becomes usable for reasoning models.
ranked.outcome_b: Size: RTN, stochastic rounding and matched Gaussian noise inflate length by the same amount at matched output error. Then inflation is predictable offline from teacher-forced total variation for weights, only lower output error helps, and the residue question about one predictive quantity is answered for the weight case.
ranked.design_it_points_to: What a 4-bit quantizer for reasoning models should minimise: output squared error, or the mean shift of layer outputs.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-4B (nine published CTIR values to check against), INT4 group 128, weights stored dequantized so vLLM runs them at full-precision speed. Arms: RTN; stochastic rounding, 3 draws; RTN plus per-output-channel bias correction from 128 calibration sequences; Gaussian weight noise matched to RTN in per-layer output squared error, 3 draws; and a null arm (same full-precision model, different batch composition). 200 MATH-500 and GPQA questions, greedy, 32k cap. Measure median and mean reasoning length, cap hits, accuracy, teacher-forced total variation, and mean logit shift at the end-of-thinking token and at marker tokens. Optional arm: quantize only the last four blocks. Stop if RTN, stochastic rounding and matched Gaussian noise all land within the spread of the null arm of each other: the size reading holds and there is no quantizer change to make.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Builds on residue (a) and is near earlier Q05 (which lossy techniques lengthen reasoning). It differs by asking which property of the weight error matters, with an intervention, not which offline quantity correlates. Sibling harvests have the same bias-vs-size question for KV and for eviction; this is the weight version.

alt_views.question: When weight quantization, KV quantization, KV eviction or bf16 state rounding makes a reasoning model think longer, is the cause a persistent signed shift of the model's state (removable by unbiased rounding or one correction vector along its own length-control direction), or does any disturbance of enough size lengthen thinking whatever its direction?
alt_views.expert_prediction: Persistent offsets lengthen thinking and fresh zero-mean noise of the same norm mostly does not; direction matters only weakly, because stopping needs a narrow state and any persistent offset misses it. So the shift along the halt direction would explain a minority of the length change across methods.
alt_views.first_experiment: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B (halt-vector recipe is published for layer 18) and Qwen3-8B, 200 MATH-500 problems x 4 samples at T=0.6, PyTorch hooks. Arms at three matched norms: fresh Gaussian noise per step; a fixed random-direction offset; a fixed offset along plus and minus the halt direction. Real methods: 4-bit KV with round-to-nearest versus stochastic rounding on the same grid, AWQ 4-bit and 3-bit weights, SnapKV and R-KV at budget 1024. Measure length ratio against a seed-noise floor, teacher-forced projection shift on the halt direction and off-axis norm for each real method, then subtract the measured shift and re-measure length. Stop if fresh noise lengthens as much as a fixed offset at equal norm and the projection shift rank-correlates with length ratio below 0.3 across the real methods: then no single quantity or debiasing design exists.

alt_views.question: Is reasoning-length inflation caused by error that repeats in the same direction over many steps, rather than by the per-step size of the error, so that randomising the error at equal size removes it?
alt_views.expert_prediction: Per-step error size (missing attention or KL) is what matters; randomising which pages are visible lowers recall and does not help, and may hurt.
alt_views.first_experiment: Qwen3-4B, AIME 30x8, 16K cap. Arm 1: existing deterministic selector at budget 512. Arm 2: pages sampled in proportion to selector score, budget raised until teacher-forced missing attention equals arm 1. Arm 3: same set frozen for 64 steps with budget raised to the same missing attention (more persistent). Arms 4-5: int4 KV with round-to-nearest vs stochastic rounding. Measure cap-hit rate, length, accuracy. Stop if arm 2 and arm 3 have the same cap-hit rate within the bootstrap interval and stochastic rounding does not beat round-to-nearest.

reasons.unpredictable: I lean toward size (matched Gaussian noise inflates about as much as RTN) at roughly 60-65%, since any fixed weight perturbation is 'persistent' and the always-positive sign can come from an asymmetric response to noise. The recurrent-state result and the HQQ-vs-RTN gap keep the bias reading alive.
reasons.generative: A gives a changed quantizer objective (mean shift, bias correction) that is cheap and data-free; B says only lower output error helps and yields an offline predictor, i.e. a number, not a method.
reasons.reviewer: Testing bias versus size of weight-quantization error for reasoning-length inflation by intervention is new for weights (2611.12127 did it for state only) and could give a data-free fix. Query 4 shows the quantized-reasoning-inflation area is busy (2606.00206, 2606.25519, RATIO), and bias correction itself is old, so novelty depends on outcome A.
reasons.feasible: Dequantized-weight variants of Qwen3-4B run at full speed in stock vLLM, and each arm is a simple weight transform. Matching the Gaussian noise per layer needs a short calibration pass; 200 questions per arm finish in under two GPU-days.

ranked.question: What sets the time of a decode attention kernel when each request reads only a short KV list, and where is the knee below which reading more tokens costs nothing?

evidence.claim: At batch 1 the sparse kernel stops speeding up after 100x sparsity; 5x fewer bytes buy 9%.
evidence.quote_or_number: B=1 speedup over FlashInfer: 100x sparsity 10.25, 200x 11.05, 500x 11.14 (dense 0.19 ms)

evidence.claim: The composable shared-prefix kernel reads about 6x fewer tokens at prefix 1024 / batch 16 and is 3% faster.
evidence.quote_or_number: prefix 1024, suffix 128: composable 45.17 us vs single 46.52 us (BS=16); prefix 8192: 88.67 vs 226.57 us (BS=16)

evidence.claim: No single kernel is efficient on both the short draft list and the full verification list.
evidence.quote_or_number: kernel optimized for verification (full) attention achieves near 85% bandwidth but less than 50% for draft (sparse) attention; kernels optimized for sparse attention deliver over 80% bandwidth, but degrade to 50% on full attention

evidence.claim: SparseSpec's own cost formula predicts more than it measures: at the reported acceptance the formula gives (6.16+1)/(8 x 0.05+1) = 5.1x (my arithmetic), the table shows 3.29x.
evidence.quote_or_number: Attention 17.1 ms -> 5.2 ms; 'reduces the execution time of Attention by 3.29x'; acceptance '6.16 out of 8 tokens'

evidence.claim: A 2026 paper names launch count and intermediates as the cause for short query batches.
evidence.quote_or_number: the query batch is larger than single-token decoding but still too small to amortize repeated kernel launches and intermediate materialization

evidence.claim: But cutting launches 8x on a small card buys only 4 to 8% at batch 8, which says launches are not the main term there.
evidence.quote_or_number: reduces launch fan-out from 16.00 to 2.00 launches per decode step; 1.044-1.080x on B8; 1.403x on a B1 bucketed trace

evidence.claim: FlashInfer itself reports that kernel-level gains shrink when the lists are short.
evidence.quote_or_number: Smaller values of n do not benefit from composable formats due to insufficient increase in block size.

ranked.expert_prediction: The floor is a stream-count limit: one short list is handled by one or a few thread blocks, each of which can only pull a fixed number of bytes per second, so a small batch of short lists cannot fill the memory bus. The knee is where lists x blocks per list saturates the card, a few hundred to a few thousand tokens per request at batch 16 to 64.
ranked.why_uncertain: Three other explanations fit the same numbers: fixed launch and planning cost per call (SSV's claim, weakened by PersistentKV's 4-8%), per-list fixed work (page-table reads, partial-tile handling, the split and merge step), and latency-bound first touches where a short list never reaches steady-state streaming. They predict different shapes: launch cost is constant in batch, stream-count scales with batch and is fixed by splitting a list across blocks, latency-bound cost scales with list count but not with splitting. Nobody has separated them, and the answer may differ between GDDR6 and HBM cards.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: 'attention kernel latency floor short KV list sparse draft speculative decoding kernel launch overhead'. Read FlashInfer, 2605.24168, SparseSpec, SSV intro, Hydragen; abstracts of PersistentKV 2606.26666, SparseSpec-L 2607.27735, Windowed-MTP 2607.21535.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: SSV (2605.19893) and PersistentKV (2606.26666) each fix one suspected cause (fusion, launch fan-out) and report end numbers; neither decomposes the floor or gives the knee. FlashInfer's Table 5 shows the effect without explaining it.
ranked.outcome_a: The floor is a stream-count or latency limit inside the kernel: then a short-list kernel that splits each list across blocks (or interleaves lists in one block) recovers the predicted 5x for sparse drafts, and sparse attention at 50-250x becomes worth having at small batch.
ranked.outcome_b: The floor is fixed per call or per list and cannot be removed: then the draft budget should be raised to the knee for free (more draft tokens kept, higher acceptance at the same time), and sparsity beyond the knee is pointless. One builds a budget rule: choose s so the list sits at the knee.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a small-list attention kernel with intra-list parallelism, or a rule that sets the sparse or draft budget at the measured knee instead of at the accuracy limit.
ranked.first_experiment: On one RTX 6000 Ada with FlashInfer's batch decode kernel and synthetic KV (Hkv=8, G=4, D=128, page 16): sweep tokens per request from 64 to 32768 and batch from 1 to 128, measuring kernel time with the plan excluded and inside a CUDA graph. Fit time = c0 + c1 x lists + bytes / BW_eff(batch). Then repeat with each list split into 2, 4 and 8 sub-lists merged afterwards, to test the stream-count explanation. Stop if the fit gives c0 and c1 below 5 us in total, i.e. the floor does not reproduce on Ada with the plan excluded; then it was host or launch overhead already addressed by SSV and PersistentKV.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Partly D3-shaped (it is a measurement on one GPU), but D3 looked for a bottleneck in the whole vLLM step and this targets one kernel regime that three papers report and none explains. It is also what limited SparseSpec's attention gain, which is the user's own system.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict a mix of per-list fixed work and too few thread blocks per short list, with sub-list splitting recovering part of the floor. Four explanations are live and the proportions are not guessable, but the qualitative lean (kernel-side under-parallelism) is common.
reasons.generative: A gives a short-list attention kernel with intra-list parallelism that recovers the sparse-draft gain; B gives a rule to set the draft budget at the measured knee, which is weaker (a setting) but still changes how SparseSpec budgets are chosen.
reasons.reviewer: The short-list kernel floor is reported by three papers and explained by none, and 'set the sparse budget at the kernel knee' is a good co-design idea. It is still profiling-shaped, and SSV and PersistentKV already attack the same floor.
reasons.feasible: A FlashInfer batch-decode sweep on synthetic KV with the plan excluded, a three-term fit, and the split-list test via existing merge-state kernels is achievable in a few days on one card.

ranked.question: When KV eviction makes a reasoning model think longer, does the extra thinking come after the answer has already formed, and does the model then fail to stop because it lost the derivation it re-reads or because it lost the record that it already checked?

evidence.claim: Under eviction the runs that finish are about as accurate as with the full cache; the loss is runs that never stop. The paper's reading of which tokens matter is interpretive, and it shows one worked example of a run that has the answer and cannot stop.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the generations that finish are wrong about as often as without eviction"; Qwen-7B MATH-500 K=1024 errors/cap hits/terminated wrong: none 104/55/49, RaaS 149/99/50, H2O 172/124/48; "Accuracy follows the tokens the model is still reading when it decides to stop."

evidence.claim: Another paper reads the eviction loss as missing information that a full-context helper can supply (abstract only).
evidence.quote_or_number: "An evicted 7B model and a full-context 1.5B model make complementary errors, and an oracle choice between their answers recovers 79% of the accuracy gap to the full-KV 7B model."

evidence.claim: A third paper guesses that eviction removes the record of a completed check, and does not test it. Its loop-detector rescue recovered few runs.
evidence.quote_or_number: "eviction deletes the record of a check along with the result."; "wait" per thousand tokens 6.4 (SnapKV-D) vs 3.7 (FullKV); rescue recovered 15% of capped runs

evidence.claim: A fourth account blames eviction of large-magnitude value states (abstract only); EpiKV reports that protecting them does nothing.
evidence.quote_or_number: VaSE: evicting them "causes catastrophic failure where models enter repetitive reasoning loops"; EpiKV: protecting them "changes neither loops nor accuracy"

evidence.claim: Lengthening under eviction is broad, not only capped loops, and has no stated mechanism.
evidence.quote_or_number: 399 of 500 problems (79.8%) longer under R-KV at 25%; "a smaller cache leads the model to generate more tokens, partly canceling the saving."

evidence.claim: Under weight quantization, about half of the failures had already reached the right answer mid-trace.
evidence.quote_or_number: "models reach the right answer in intermediate reasoning steps but do not output it as a final answer" in "up to 52%" of failures

evidence.claim: A forced-readout method exists for locating where the answer forms, and in an unperturbed model more than half the thinking comes after it.
evidence.quote_or_number: "54% of thinking tokens on the hard set and 64% on the confirmation set come after that point"

ranked.expert_prediction: Most of the extra thinking comes after the answer has formed, and the model fails to stop mainly because the derivation it wants to re-read is gone, not because its own check statements are gone.
ranked.why_uncertain: EpiKV's evidence is greedy decoding on two R1 distills at one budget plus one example. ReCo's lengthening hits 79.8% of problems under sampling, which looks like slower derivation, not only failed stopping. KV-Rescue reads the loss as missing information. Four papers name four different sets of tokens the stop decision depends on, and none masks them in a controlled way. The part of EpiKV beyond 100,000 characters (Appendix E.1) was not read and may bear on loop onset.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: "KV cache" AND reasoning AND (re-derive OR recompute OR re-verification OR loop) -> 2606.03928; epiphany AND "KV cache" -> 2606.26472; KV AND rescue AND reasoning AND eviction -> 2608.15797; KV AND reasoning AND eviction AND longer -> 2610.20641, 2603.11504, 2512.12008, 2512.07993; reasoning AND KV AND eviction AND answer AND verification AND stop -> nothing; "reasoning models" AND loop AND why -> 2512.12895, 2607.11317.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: EpiKV (2606.26472): shows the loss is non-termination and that keeping recently read tokens reduces cap hits, but does not locate the extra tokens relative to answer formation and does not separate derivation tokens from check-record tokens.
ranked.outcome_a: Post-answer, and the tail needs only its own recent output: the derivation is disposable once the answer forms. Build commit-then-drop: on a commitment signal evict the derivation wholesale and keep the problem, the answer statement and the tail. KV saving and early exit are then different savings and stack.
ranked.outcome_b: Post-answer, and the tail re-reads the derivation: the verification pass is the main reader of old KV, so eviction and early exit claim the same saving. Remove the tail (exit or concise training) and old KV has no reader; keep the tail and it cannot be evicted. Build exit at answer formation instead of better selectors. If the extra tokens are instead before the answer, eviction gain on reasoning is bounded by recomputation and the selector route (killed D1) should stay closed.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Commitment-triggered eviction of the derivation, or exit-at-commit as the replacement for eviction on reasoning workloads.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B and R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, 200 hard MATH-500 and AIME problems, T=0.6, 4 seeds. Step 1: run full cache and SnapKV / R-KV at budget 1024; close thinking every 512 tokens and read the answer to find where it first equals the final answer and stays; split the excess length into before and after. Step 2: on full-cache traces, 256 tokens after the answer forms, fork with attention masked to (a) derivation tokens before the answer, problem kept; (b) post-answer tokens except the last 64; (c) a random set of equal size; 4 continuations each; measure remaining thinking length, cap hits and answer changes. Stop if less than a third of the excess is post-answer and the three masks do not differ.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near D1 (the perturbation is KV eviction on long reasoning) and near two earlier questions: 'extra tokens: compensation or symptom' and Q07 (offline metric for non-termination). It differs by asking which part of the trace the stop decision reads and by using masked forks on full-cache traces; it proposes no selector. The pre-answer branch of outcome B would lead back into D1 and should not be pursued.

reasons.unpredictable: I cannot confidently say whether the excess is mostly post-answer under eviction (ReCo's 79.8% lengthening under sampling suggests slower derivation too) or which token set the stop decision reads. Four papers name four different sets and no masked-fork data exists.
reasons.generative: A gives commitment-triggered wholesale eviction of the derivation; B gives exit-at-commit as the replacement for eviction. Both are concrete policies, though a third branch (excess is pre-answer) leads back into killed D1 and ends.
reasons.reviewer: Masked forks to find what the stop decision reads are clean, and commit-then-drop eviction is a concrete design. Reasoning-KV eviction is crowded (EpiKV, R-KV, ReCo, KV-Rescue, 2608.04771) and one branch leads back into D1.
reasons.feasible: Step 1 needs eviction runs (SnapKV/R-KV, slow HF-based code) on 200 problems x 4 seeds with forced readouts every 512 tokens. Step 2 adds masked forks with four continuations each; together about two weeks, although the masks are easy via past attention masks.

ranked.question: When a GDN/Mamba recurrent state is written back with round-to-nearest, is the harm (longer reasoning, repetition loops) caused by rounding the decay term or by rounding the writes, and why do KL-based papers point at the slowest heads while the only behavioural localisation finds them inert?

evidence.claim: The behavioural failure is rounding bias, and on Nemotron-Nano it sits in an intermediate-decay band, not in the heads with the largest teacher-forced KL.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models... so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution"; "SR on 25% of heads (an intermediate-decay band) removes the effect, while random heads and the top teacher-forced-KL octiles do not; in Nemotron-3 and Qwen3.5-9B the effect is spread across heads."

evidence.claim: The slowest decay octile holds about half of teacher-forced KL but fixing it does nothing for length; the paper's decay toy model does not predict which heads matter and fails on Qwen3.5-9B.
evidence.source: Lost in Rounding (arXiv 2611.12127), body (HTML via WebFetch)
evidence.quote_or_number: Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 TF-KL share by decay octile: q0 49%, q1 37%, q2 15%. SR on q1+q2 (864 heads, 25%, decay 0.57u to 4.1u): F_log 1.03 [0.86, 1.23]; SR on q0 alone: -0.12; top-2 KL octiles 0.59; random 864 heads 0.06. Band test on Qwen3.5-9B: F_log 0.35. "Why their freezing does not change behaviour remains open." The toy "does not predict which heads matter".

evidence.claim: A different paper explains RTN failure by lost small writes rather than frozen decay, finds the gain in long-memory entries, and measures only KL. Its lemma lumps decay and write into one update.
evidence.source: Low-Discrepancy Dither for quantized recurrent state (arXiv 2609.39185), abstract and body
evidence.quote_or_number: "Round-to-nearest behaves differently: because it discards small updates, its error keeps growing"; Lemma 1 uses the combined update "δt = (at−1)ĥt−1+wt"; dither on the top 25% of entries by memory keeps "75–87% of the full gain"; with rounding every 8th write the advantage "mostly disappeared on the hybrids"; the paper "measures KL rather than generation length or task accuracy".

evidence.claim: Low-bit state allocators give extra precision to the longest-lived (slowest) heads, the group the behavioural paper found inert.
evidence.quote_or_number: "longer-lived state units tend to exhibit larger accumulated errors"; Spearman about 0.80 between gate half-life and accumulated state error across 2304 heads under uniform INT6; "uniform quantization substantially increases output length"; Kimi INT4 AIME output 63.40K tokens.

evidence.claim: Two more quantizers protect slow heads and/or round less often, each with its own stated reason.
evidence.quote_or_number: LoReS: "decay-based mixed-precision to protect slowly decaying heads or channels, and stochastic rounding to limit error accumulation under repeated requantization". PACE: "PACE rounds the state only once every few generated tokens"; "Rounding less often reduces the error that accumulates in the state"; "It also keeps the heads that retain rounding error longest at eight bits."

evidence.claim: A third line fixes low-bit GDN state by keeping recent writes apart from the old state, and says the retention mechanism is not characterised.
evidence.source: Low-bit GDN state with pure-write window (arXiv 2610.39931), body
evidence.quote_or_number: "We have not yet fully characterized how information written by tokens is retained and read during state recurrences"; window m = 8 only; STEP@44+PW-S8 beats STEP@55 by 3.29 (4B) and 1.57 (9B) points; cap-hit rate at @44 falls from 36.66%/30.67% (STEP) to 4.61%/2.44% (GGA+PW-S8).

evidence.claim: Rounding once per window is said to reduce error, and separating read precision from update precision is said to break a feedback loop; all arms already use stochastic rounding, so the RTN case is untested.
evidence.quote_or_number: "A shared checkpoint is requantized once per window, so its error falls as L grows"; "Separate precisions break the feedback loop"; shared NVFP4+SR: -5.88 / -13.05 / -10.92 points; NVFP4 read with FP16 update +SR: -0.15 / -2.36 / -0.10 (MMLU-Pro / GPQA-Diamond / Math-L5).

evidence.claim: States are dominated by a few stable directions, which is the condition under which a small write lands on a large entry; that paper has no precision result.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the queries, keys, and values of linear layers concentrate in a stable, low-dimensional subspace, a phenomenon we call the linear attention sink"; PG-19 top-1 direction 39-74%, top-8 73-88%; "The recurrent states are kept in FP32 for all models".

ranked.expert_prediction: Round-to-nearest absorbs small increments, error piles up most in slow-decaying heads, and any unbiased or deferred rounding fixes it; decay and write are two views of one accumulated error.
ranked.why_uncertain: The one paper that localises the behavioural effect (length, loops) finds the slowest octile inert (-0.12) although it carries 49% of teacher-forced KL, and its own decay-band account fails on Qwen3.5-9B. The decay toy predicts that the harmful band scales with tokens per writeback (writing every 8-16 tokens should move the 0.57u-4.1u band out of the distorted zone under plain RTN); the lost-write account predicts the interval matters much less than the size of the entry a write lands on. Nobody has separated the two terms.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search "recurrent state rounding hybrid linear attention precision" (2 results: PACE 2610.29545, LeapQuant 2609.38166). WebSearch "recurrent state bf16 round-to-nearest bias decay stagnation small writes absorbed" (found 2609.39185). Read bodies of 2611.12127, 2609.39185, 2609.38169, 2610.39931, 2610.13778, 2611.14246 for a decay-vs-write split, a writeback-interval test under RTN, or a rank/sink analysis: none found. arXiv API keyword search and Semantic Scholar were rate-limited, so citation-graph follow-ups were not checked.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: Lost in Rounding (2611.12127) for behaviour and head localisation; Low-Discrepancy Dither (2609.39185) for the lost-write account and an interval-8 result, but KL only, on 130M-1.4B models, and with decay and write combined.
ranked.outcome_a: Decay term is the cause: keep the per-head decay as an exact scalar outside the stored matrix (lazy scaling; the GDN and Mamba-2 decay is one scalar per head, my inference from the update rule, not from a paper), so the matrix is rounded only on writes and no random numbers are needed; windowed writeback alone should fix RTN; allocators should protect the intermediate band, not the slowest heads.
ranked.outcome_b: Write term is the cause: split off the dominant directions (sink subspace, compensator tokens) and round only the residual, or keep recent writes in a side buffer; allocate bits by write-to-entry ratio instead of lifetime; KL-ranked head protection is the wrong target and a drift-based offline metric replaces it.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A sub-8-bit recurrent-state format whose protected set and structure (exact scalar decay vs sink/residual split) follow from the measured cause, plus an offline metric (signed state drift by term) that predicts length inflation where teacher-forced KL does not. This also feeds residue (a).
ranked.first_experiment: Offline: record FP32 per-token decay, gate, key and value streams for every GDN/Mamba head of Qwen3.5-9B and Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2 on about 50 long reasoning traces. Replay each head with bf16 RTN and FP8 RTN in arms: round everything; exact decay with rounded writes; rounded decay with exact writes; writeback every 1, 4, 16 tokens. Measure signed drift of state norm and of the readout, split by decay octile and by top-8 subspace vs residual. Online: FP32, bf16 RTN, bf16 SR, and the two arms that differ most, on about 150 competition-math problems, counting cap hits, repetition loops and length. Stop if neither exact-decay nor exact-write removes at least half of what SR removes offline, or if the bf16-RTN/FP32 length ratio on this setup is inside the seed spread.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Not D1-D4. Near earlier-search questions on state error in low-energy directions, state magnitude vs bf16, and step vs chunked scan; near sibling own-projects card on persistent vs per-step error; feeds residue (a). Differs by asking which term and which heads, using the contradiction between the Nov 2026 papers.
