Caveat: stochastic rounding already fixes bf16 at no cost, so the payoff is at 8 bits and below and in the choice of metric.

reasons.unpredictable: Both terms have a solid first-principles failure mode (decay absorbed when (1-a)|S| is below half an ulp; small writes absorbed into large entries), and the behavioural localisation contradicts the KL ranking. I lean slightly to the decay term but could not defend it.
reasons.generative: A gives an exact-scalar lazy-decay state format with windowed writeback; B gives a sink/residual split or side buffer with a write-ratio bit allocator, plus a drift metric either way. The payoff is narrowed because stochastic rounding already fixes bf16.
reasons.reviewer: The KL-versus-behaviour contradiction in head localisation is real and the decay/write split is untested. Stochastic rounding already fixes bf16, and recurrent state is small, so sub-8-bit state formats have a limited audience.
reasons.feasible: The offline per-head replay of recorded decay/gate/key/value streams is doable in a week. The online arms (exact-decay versus exact-write rounding, FP32 state) need modified GDN and Mamba state-update kernels or slow PyTorch generation on two different hybrid codebases.

ranked.question: Are the tokens whose values cannot be predicted from their keys the tokens that later queries read, or only the tokens with the largest reconstruction error?

evidence.claim: Which tokens get exact values decides almost everything, and attention-output error does not explain it.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Random selection scores less than 40%, with or without sinks, whereas MSE-ranked selection recovers 98%. Forcing residuals for attention sinks reduces attention-output error for both random and MSE-ranked selection but does not positively affect accuracy." (RULER NIAH-Multikey-1, 4K tokens, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct)

evidence.claim: A small set of hard-to-predict tokens carries a third of the performance; their stability is unknown.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Removing residual corrections drops recovered performance from 99.0% to 64.9% (34.1 points)"; "It is also unclear ... whether hard-to-predict tokens are stable across contexts"

evidence.claim: A predictability-based signal (what a reread cannot predict) fails as an importance score on natural text.
evidence.quote_or_number: "At a 3% keep ratio, rereading the whole context keeps 31.5 of 96.5 points on RULER"; "in natural text nearly every token is unpredictable, and a full reread spreads the budget evenly. The answer-aware oracle keeps 48.4% on average."

evidence.claim: A cheap key-geometry signal is used successfully to pick anchors.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the keys that stand out from the chunk's average key are the anchors"

evidence.claim: In trained caches keys route and values carry the content.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Cartridge keys act as stable, shareable retrieval routers for the compressed corpora and ... most of the learned compression occurs within the Cartridge value vectors"

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly a benchmark artifact. In needle-in-a-haystack the needle is an outlier for a predictor fitted on the haystack, so error-ranked selection finds it for free. On natural text, key-to-value unpredictability will track what gets asked only weakly.
ranked.why_uncertain: If keys are addresses and values are content, a value the key does not imply is exactly the information the token adds beyond its address, which is close to what a fact is. Attic's key-outlier anchor rule does work on natural text. LowRAM's 34-point drop without residuals is over its whole benchmark suite, not only the synthetic task.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: abs:"KV cache" AND ("from keys" OR "from the keys" OR "key-to-value" OR "predict values" OR "values from keys") returned only LowRAM among relevant hits. Read LowRAM's selection ablation, Attic-KV sections 3-4, KVzip introduction.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: LowRAM's own residual-selection ablation (one synthetic task, no comparison with any importance score) and Attic-KV's measurement of how much of the answer's KV each rehearsal keeps. Neither compares key-to-value residual with what future queries attend to.
ranked.outcome_a: It is an importance signal: a query-agnostic eviction score from one closed-form regression per head, with no second pass over the context (KVzip) and no generated questions (Attic).
ranked.outcome_b: It is independent of importance: predictability and importance are two axes and the savings multiply. Evict unimportant tokens, store keys only for important and predictable ones, store full entries for the rest. It also tells anyone composing LowRAM with eviction that the synthetic-task number does not transfer.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a forward-free query-agnostic eviction scorer, or a two-axis (importance by predictability) cache layout.
ranked.first_experiment: Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Data: SQuAD multi-question contexts (KVzip's setting), LongBench QA, RULER NIAH 4K. Per head, fit a closed-form ridge map from keys to values per context. Compare the per-token residual norm with (a) oracle attention from held-out question and answer tokens, (b) the KVzip score, (c) key distance from the chunk mean, (d) value norm, by Spearman correlation and overlap at 10%. Then evict to 10-30% by residual and compare with KVzip and SnapKV on multi-query QA. Stop if overlap with the oracle on natural text is within 1.2x of chance; that settles outcome B in about two days.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: None. This is prefill-time, query-agnostic scoring, not D1 decode-time page selection.

reasons.unpredictable: I lean toward a weak-to-moderate correlation on natural text (content tokens such as entities and numbers have both unusual values and more question attention), not pure artifact and not a usable scorer. The needle confound makes most experts lean 'artifact', but with doubt.
reasons.generative: A gives a forward-free query-agnostic eviction scorer from a closed-form regression; B's two-axis cache layout is speculative and the likely reading of B is simply 'the signal does not transfer'.
reasons.reviewer: Key-to-value residual as a query-agnostic importance score is a fresh idea and cheap to test. The expert reading (needle-benchmark artifact) is probably right, and the fallback two-axis layout is a weak paper.
reasons.feasible: A closed-form ridge fit per head and context and a rank-correlation against held-out question attention is a two-day experiment on Llama-3.1-8B with public data. KVzip and SnapKV code are public for the follow-up eviction comparison.

ranked.question: For the same context tokens in a GDN hybrid, is the recurrent state's record redundant with the KV entry (so evicting the KV entry is partly covered) or do the two work in series (so losing either loses the token)?

evidence.claim: Whole-context ablation: exact retrieval goes only through attention; language and persona go mostly through the recurrent state.
evidence.source: What Attention Recalls and Recurrence Controls (arXiv 2609.04434), abstract and Table 1
evidence.quote_or_number: "Exact retrieval survives only through attention (64–98% of full accuracy) and collapses to zero through recurrence." Qwen3.5-4B rec-only / kv-only: KV retrieve 0.00 / 0.89; language following 0.70 / 0.01; persona 0.49 / 0.14. "The recurrent state preserves the semantic field of seen words rather than their identities." Limitation: "Split-prefill resets one cache while preserving the other, which produces a partly out-of-distribution combination."

evidence.claim: A serial account: the recurrent layers build the query and attention answers it, which predicts no compensation.
evidence.quote_or_number: "linear attention constructs the query, while softmax attention performs the lookup"

evidence.claim: Stock hybrids lean on attention, but a small LoRA with an auxiliary loss moves a lot of the load into the state, so the capacity exists.
evidence.quote_or_number: "we find a substantially greater reliance on attention than on the recurrent state"; Qwen3.5-4B QA: Full 30.2%, Attention-only 20.2%, Recurrent-only 5.1%; with LoRA rank 16 and auxiliary loss: Recurrent-only 5.0% to 22.8%, Attention-only 25.0% to 23.7%.

evidence.claim: Hybrid KV eviction methods keep the tokens that write most strongly to the state, and score utility on attention output, not on logits; none tests whether the state still carries an evicted token.
evidence.quote_or_number: Utility is "how much removing it changes the attention output over the model's own continuations"; "useful entries tend to arrive where the recurrent state updates more strongly"; top decile of slow-head β‖v‖ reaches the top utility decile 18.2% of the time (1.82x chance); forgetting correlates +0.06 to +0.19 with utility.

evidence.claim: Two other hybrid eviction papers use the same keep-what-the-state-writes rule while describing the two memories as complementary.
evidence.quote_or_number: DeltaS keeps chunks "inducing larger normalized state change"; "the two memories of hybrid architectures can work cooperatively." HOLA: "the cache stores associations that should not be forced through that state", keeping "tokens with large beta * ||e||, the prediction residual actually committed to the state".

evidence.claim: Own data: per unit of missing attention the hybrid's next-token distribution moves far less offline, but the advantage vanished online, and a GDN write-gate prior barely predicts attention mass.
evidence.source: kv-fetch EXPERIMENTS.md, H-b and H-d (own project)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Qwen3.5's oracle@512 gives next-token KL 0.011 at 22.9% missing; Qwen3-4B 0.035 at 14.1%"; "7.4-7.5x lower KL over three pairs with matched missing attention (confounded: 8 perturbed layers vs 36)"; "H-b FAILED online: prompt-protected SnapKV@1K loses 40.0 points on Qwen3.5 vs 38.8 on Qwen3-4B (ratio 1.03, needed <= 0.5)"; GDN prior Spearman with page mass "0.09 (beta) / -0.01 (forgot)".

ranked.expert_prediction: Little compensation on stock models: the state does not hold token identity, so evicting a KV entry costs about what the attention change predicts, for every token type.
ranked.why_uncertain: Persona and output-language instructions are delivered almost entirely by the state (0.70 vs 0.01), so for those tokens the KV entry may be dead weight; the state keeps a semantic field, which may be enough for restated reasoning; a rank-16 LoRA moves recurrent-only QA from 5.0% to 22.8%; and own offline KL per unit of missing attention is 7.4-7.5x lower on the hybrid. Against all that, the serial query-then-lookup account predicts the opposite sign. The existing evidence is whole-context ablation, which the authors themselves call partly out of distribution; nobody has done it per token group.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search "hybrid recurrent state KV cache eviction attention" (3 results: HiState 2610.41508, DeltaS 2609.27470, DASC 2608.30386). WebSearch on whether the recurrent state compensates for evicted KV tokens in hybrid models (found HOLA 2607.02303, DeltaS, 2510.20787). Read bodies of 2610.14754, 2609.04434, 2610.06750 for a selective (token-level) two-pathway ablation: none.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2609.04434 (split-prefill, whole context, not selective) and GateSight 2610.14754 (state signals predict KV utility, but utility is measured on attention output and compensation is not tested).
ranked.outcome_a: Redundant for a class of tokens (for example system prompt, style or language instructions, restated reasoning): a hybrid-only eviction budget that drops state-covered tokens first; attention-output utility as used by GateSight over-counts those tokens; an offline state-recoverability score becomes the selector feature that dense models cannot have.
ranked.outcome_b: In series (interaction positive or zero): KV eviction on hybrids has no hybrid-specific slack and the D1 result is explained rather than just observed; effort should go to compressing entries (quantization, low rank) instead of dropping them, and the auxiliary-loss LoRA of 2610.06750 is the only way to buy slack.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a token-class-aware eviction policy for hybrids driven by state coverage, or a clear statement that hybrids need compression not eviction, with the LoRA rebalancing as the follow-up arm.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B, teacher-forced, about 100 reasoning traces and 100 long-prompt QA items. For 64-token chunks run four conditions: intact; chunk masked from attention only; chunk's writes removed from all GDN states only (write gate zeroed for those tokens); both. Measure continuation NLL and take the interaction term (both minus the sum of the singles): negative means redundant, positive means in series. Split by token type (system prompt, problem statement, thinking, tool output). Stop if the interaction is under 10% of the larger single effect for every token type.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near D1 (killed): this does not propose a selector, it asks the hybrid-specific reason D1's hybrid advantage did not appear. Near earlier Q23 and the sibling own-projects card on where an attention error goes in a hybrid; that card tracks how one error decays over time, this one asks whether the state holds a second copy. Not D2 (no checkpoints or prefix caching).

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict little compensation for most token types and clear redundancy for instruction/persona-style tokens, which the published split-prefill numbers (0.70 vs 0.01) already suggest. The per-chunk interaction sign for reasoning text is the uncertain part.
reasons.generative: A gives a hybrid-only eviction policy driven by a state-recoverability score; B explains D1's failure and says 'compress, do not evict', which ends the eviction line without a new method.
reasons.reviewer: The 2x2 mask-attention versus remove-state-write interaction per token class is a clean causal test nobody has run, and hybrids like Qwen3.5 are now mainstream. Either result is usable: a hybrid-only eviction policy, or a mechanistic reason eviction has no hybrid slack.
reasons.feasible: The four-condition chunk ablation is teacher-forced on 4B and 9B hybrids and fits one card. Zeroing the write gate for selected tokens needs a patched PyTorch GDN forward, a moderate build.

ranked.question: Is the extra reasoning length caused by a lossy variant (weight quantization, KV quantization, KV eviction) determined by its teacher-forced divergence rate, on one curve across the three families, or by what the model does after the first divergence?

evidence.claim: Most accumulated token mismatch under eviction comes after the first divergence, not from when it happens.
evidence.source: Divergence Timing and Cumulative Disagreement under KV-Cache Eviction (arXiv 2609.16617), abstract
evidence.quote_or_number: "post-divergence exposure accounts for 85-90% of four aggregate mismatch gaps"

evidence.claim: Lossy KV (eviction and quantization alike) diverges from the full model at a steady per-step rate.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Sequence-level KL KL(p_full(x_1:t) ∥ p_lossy(x_1:t)) grows roughly linearly in t under KVzip 4× (left) and TurboQuant k4v3 (right); at temperature 0.5."

evidence.claim: Eviction keeps task accuracy but lengthens generation, more for weaker selectors.
evidence.quote_or_number: "eviction generally lengthens generation relative to full attention, most for the weakest s[electors]" (sentence continues past my excerpt)

evidence.claim: A token-level difference rate does not tell you how much the difference matters.
evidence.quote_or_number: "A model's certainty about a token predicts how likely it is to differ from the full model's choice, but not how much that difference affects judged quality."

evidence.claim: One offline number (perplexity degradation) is claimed to predict acceptance of a degraded self-drafter.
evidence.source: Component-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding in Hybrid Language Models (arXiv 2605.01106), abstract
evidence.quote_or_number: "perplexity degradation from a companion ablation study predicts speculative viability without running speculative decoding: a 3.15x ratio (Falcon) maps to alpha = 0.37 at k=4, while 81.96x (Qwen) maps to alpha = 0.019"

evidence.claim: For quantization, high-KL positions are reported to coincide with hesitation tokens.
evidence.source: Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not (arXiv 2606.00206)
evidence.quote_or_number: From a web search summary, not from the paper: the ratio of high-KL hesitation tokens to low-KL math tokens rises from 0.57 to 1.15 under 3-bit AWQ.

ranked.expert_prediction: No single curve. Quantization noise is spread over many tokens and nudges the model toward hesitation; eviction removes specific facts and forces re-derivation. The same divergence rate would give different length inflation in the two families.
ranked.why_uncertain: The opposite is plausible. Per-step divergence is steady for both KV eviction and KV quantization (VeriCache), and length inflation tracks selector quality (Random Attention), which is what a single hazard curve would produce. Against that, 85 to 90% of mismatch is post-divergence, which a teacher-forced number cannot see. Nobody has put the three families on one axis.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search: "divergence" "generation length" reasoning quantization predict; "speculative decoding" "acceptance" "perplexity" predicts. WebSearch: per-token KL divergence predicts reasoning length inflation quantization KV cache eviction single metric 2026. Also the earlier verification notes for Q05 (citation lists of ThinKV, R-KV, SkipKV, Random Attention and others were scanned there). No paper tests one predictor across weight quantization, KV quantization and eviction.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2606.00206 gives a token-level account for weight quantization only (not read in this session). 2609.16617 decomposes mismatch for eviction only and does not look at length. DistillCache (2608.08878, seen in a web result) uses per-step KL as a training reward for eviction, not as a predictor of length.
ranked.outcome_a: One curve holds. Then the acceptance rate of the lossy variant used as a self-drafter is a universal offline score: lossy settings can be tuned teacher-forced in minutes, and since the same number gives the speedup of the verify route (VeriCache style), there is a closed-form rule for when to trust the lossy model and when to verify it.
ranked.outcome_b: No single curve; post-divergence behaviour is family-specific. Then offline fidelity metrics should not be used to compare techniques across families, and the thing to build is a detector of the costly kind of divergence (the model starts re-deriving) that triggers a one-off repair, for example a full-KV or full-precision step, instead of continuous verification.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A trust-or-verify controller for lossy inference: run lossy while the measured hazard predicts little inflation, switch to draft-and-verify when it does not. Under outcome B, a divergence-type detector plus targeted repair.
ranked.first_experiment: Model Qwen3-8B (repeat on Qwen3-4B if time allows). Variants: AWQ 4-bit and 3-bit weights; KV quantization at 4 and 2 bits; eviction with R-KV and Random Attention at 4x and 8x (the Random Attention code and vLLM integration are public). Step 1, teacher-forced on 100 full-model MATH500/AIME traces: per-token greedy disagreement rate, mean TV, mean KL. Step 2, free-running on the same 100 problems, 2 seeds: length ratio, accuracy, time of first divergence, post-divergence mismatch rate. Fit length ratio against each step-1 quantity and report leave-one-family-out error. Stop if that error exceeds three times the seed-to-seed spread for every candidate quantity: no single offline quantity exists at this resolution.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Direct continuation of residue (a) and of earlier Q05 and Q30. What is new: a named candidate quantity (the divergence hazard, equal to one minus self-draft acceptance), the first-divergence vs post-divergence split as the test that can refute it, and the link to the trust-or-verify decision. Not a load-condition question.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict no single curve: a monotone trend with family-specific offsets, since eviction and quantization differ in post-divergence behaviour (about 65% confidence). The steady per-step divergence reported for both KV families keeps the one-hazard reading possible.
reasons.generative: A gives a universal offline score and a closed-form trust-or-verify controller; B gives a divergence-type detector with one-off targeted repair. Both are designs, though B's detector is unspecified and the stop condition may yield 'no quantity exists'.
reasons.reviewer: A single hazard curve across weight quantization, KV quantization and eviction, tied to self-draft acceptance, would be a unifying result, and its refutation test (first versus post-divergence) is explicit. Query 4 confirms each family has been studied separately but not on one axis; a no-single-curve outcome yields a weaker paper.
reasons.feasible: Three technique families (AWQ weights, KV quantization, R-KV and Random Attention eviction) must run both teacher-forced and free-running. 100 problems x 2 seeds gives noisy length ratios for a leave-one-family-out fit on about eight points, and teacher-forced eviction is awkward to define.

ranked.question: Why is thinking text less draftable than answer text for the same target: because the target has more near-tied and multi-future positions when it thinks (irreducible for lossless drafting), or because drafters are trained and shaped for answer text (reducible)?

evidence.claim: Accepted length drops with thinking enabled, even with a drafter trained on reasoning traces, at temperature 0.
evidence.quote_or_number: Qwen3-8B, T=0: MATH-500 7.87 (thinking disabled) versus 5.82 (enabled); AIME25 7.08 versus 5.74; thinking drafter "trained on target-model outputs with reasoning traces"

evidence.claim: The main 2026 drafter comparison disables thinking, so the regime with most tokens is unmeasured.
evidence.quote_or_number: targets run "with thinking disabled"

evidence.claim: A reasoning distill has a lower entropy statistic than its base on math and chat but higher on code, so 'thinking is higher entropy' is not uniformly true.
evidence.quote_or_number: μ at T=1: GSM8K 0.233 (R1-distill Llama 8B) versus 0.636 (Llama-3 8B); MT-bench 0.633 versus 1.088; HumanEval 0.530 (R1-distill)

evidence.claim: A method paper asserts a drafter-type split by text kind without diagnosing it.
evidence.quote_or_number: "either autoregressive drafting models for reasoning or diffusion-based parallel drafting models for structured outputs. We empirically find that drafting accuracy fluctuates dramatically within a single sequence"

evidence.claim: Target entropy explains little of acceptance in the one study that correlated them.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the entropy-acceptance correlation is consistently negative but weak across all domains (rho in [-0.20, -0.15]). Counterintuitively, chat produces the highest entropy yet the highest acceptance rate."

evidence.claim: Trees waste nodes when two futures disagree in several positions, a pattern expected in free-form reasoning.
evidence.quote_or_number: "in practice chimeras make up 27-33% of a 64-node tree"

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly irreducible: self-talk has more positions where several phrasings are near-equally likely, so any lossless drafter hits a lower ceiling there; drafter data is a smaller factor.
ranked.why_uncertain: The published gap is at temperature 0, where nothing is irreducible by definition (a perfect drafter matches every argmax), so near-ties can only hurt through drafter error at low-margin positions. The R1-distill row shows lower target entropy on math than the base model, which would predict easier drafting. The entropy-acceptance correlation in the one direct study is weak. Nobody has split acceptance by think and answer segments for the same problems.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API query: "speculative decoding" AND (thinking OR "reasoning trace") AND acceptance; one web search on thinking-versus-answer acceptance, which returned no direct split. Read abstracts of 2604.14682, 2602.03708, 2608.20359.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: arXiv 2602.06036 reports the numbers without analysis. arXiv 2604.14682 compares task domains with a non-reasoning 7B target. arXiv 2602.03708 (SemanticSpec) and 2608.20359 (SSR) propose methods for reasoning models but do not diagnose why token-level acceptance is lower. arXiv 2606.30265 gives margin certificates that could be reused for the split.
ranked.outcome_a: If the think segment has a lower target ceiling and the same ceiling-use ratio as the answer segment: lossless drafting is bounded where most tokens are, and the lever is step-level or lossy acceptance with a controlled length cost (links to the lossy-verification card).
ranked.outcome_b: If the ceilings are similar and the gap is drafter error at confident positions: build thinking-specific drafter data, or route between autoregressive and block drafters by segment; a large gain exists where most tokens are generated.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Segment-aware drafting (B) or a decision to stop pursuing lossless gains inside thinking and move to semantic or relaxed acceptance there (A).
ranked.first_experiment: Same instrument as the ceiling card. Qwen3-8B with thinking on, the MATH-500 problems used by DFlash; mark each position as think or answer. For each segment: distribution of the target's top probability and top-2 margin; the target-only chain ceiling at T=1 for budget 16; realized accepted length of the two released DFlash drafters (thinking and non-thinking) and EAGLE-3 at T=0 and T=1; share of rejections at near-tied positions; at T=0, rejection rate as a function of target margin. Stop signal: if both segments show the same accepted length once conditioned on target margin, the gap is fully explained by the margin distribution (answer A) and no drafter-side work is indicated.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: none with D1-D4. Shares its measurement tool with the ceiling card but asks a different question (segment difference, including the temperature-0 case where the ceiling argument does not apply).

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict the margin distribution explains most of the gap (thinking has more near-tied positions and drafters fail at low margin), with a smaller drafter-data effect. The T=0 framing leaves real doubt, but most experts would lean the same way.
reasons.generative: Outcome B gives segment-aware drafter data or routing; outcome A says to stop pursuing lossless gains in thinking and hands off to another card. One productive branch, one terminating branch.
reasons.reviewer: Useful diagnostic, but derivative of the F02 instrument, and the likely answer (thinking text has thinner margins) is what most reviewers expect. Segment-aware drafting is an incremental design.
reasons.feasible: Target-only margin statistics split by think and answer, plus one released drafter at T=0, give a first signal in a few days on one card. It depends on getting the DFlash and EAGLE-3 drafters running teacher-forced at the same positions.

ranked.question: To hold a sparse self-draft's per-token acceptance fixed as the context grows, does the number of KV entries it needs stay roughly constant or grow in proportion, and is the answer different when the context is the model's own reasoning trace rather than a prompt?

evidence.claim: One benchmark study says the tolerable sparsity rises with length.
evidence.quote_or_number: longer sequences tolerate higher sparsity, suggesting that fixed-budget methods in production are suboptimal

evidence.claim: A sparse-draft paper says a fixed KV budget loses acceptance quickly between 4K and 16K context.
evidence.quote_or_number: naive sparse/full speculative decoding suffers from the sparse/full mismatch as context length grows, causing the acceptance rate to drop quickly

evidence.claim: On book continuation at 120K context, under 1% of entries is enough for very high acceptance with oracle selection.
evidence.quote_or_number: utilizing only 1K tokens could theoretically achieve a 97.6% acceptance rate with Top-K selection method

evidence.claim: On short reasoning contexts a much larger fraction gives much lower acceptance: 5% of 8K gives 80.4%; 256 of 2k gives block efficiency 3-4 of 5.
evidence.source: S3R, arXiv 2610.13202 (budget sweep); EfficientRollout, arXiv 2606.18967 (App. B.2)
evidence.quote_or_number: Increasing s from 0.05 to 0.50 raises acceptance from 80.4% to 96.7% ... retaining 256 tokens, the resulting drafter remains relatively weak: with γ=5, block efficiency τ typically stays around 3–4

evidence.claim: SparseSpec fixes a ratio and argues that in reasoning output the needed entries move; its speedup at that ratio is 6.78x in attention time. By the paper's ratio (ks+1)/(kα+1) the s->0 limit is kα+1 = 13 at k=16, α=0.75 (my arithmetic).
evidence.quote_or_number: For long output of RLMs, sparsity patterns shift significantly based on semantic context during generation. ... with k=16, α=0.75, s=0.05, the attention latency is reduced by 6.78×

evidence.claim: As generation proceeds, a prompt-time selection keeps less and less of the attention.
evidence.quote_or_number: drops from 67.0% to 25.4% for SnapKV, while increasing from 43.5% to 68.7% for SWA as generation progresses

evidence.claim: At a fixed compression ratio, acceptance is reported stable from 10K to 60K prompts.
evidence.quote_or_number: While all methods exhibit stable acceptance rates and increasing speedups at longer contexts

ranked.expert_prediction: Near-constant count for long prompts (the needed fraction falls with length), but close to proportional growth when the context is generated reasoning.
ranked.why_uncertain: The published points do not line up on either law: 1K of 120K (0.8%) gives 97.6% on book text, 400 of 8K (5%) gives 80.4% and 256 of 2k (12.5%) gives 3-4 of 5 on reasoning rollouts. Those cases differ in temperature, task and selection method at once, so the gap could be the sampler rather than the kind of context. No paper varies prompt length and generated length separately at fixed acceptance, and CVSA's finding that failures sit in a small model-dependent set of layers means the law could be set by a few layers only.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: ti:'Sparse Frontier' (2504.17768); 'sparse attention' + 'context length' + ('scaling law' OR sublinear OR 'fixed budget') (nothing relevant); 'KV cache' + compression + acceptance + draft (RIFT, 2608.30252, 2607.27269, 2604.26412); 'speculative decoding' + ('sparse attention' OR 'sparse KV') (20 hits checked). Read TriForce 3.1 and Table 2, MagicDec 4.3-4.4, S3R sweep, SparseSpec-L context-length section.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: The Sparse Frontier (2504.17768) gives the trend for task accuracy on long-prompt tasks with short answers. TriForce and SparseSpec-L show acceptance against prompt length at one budget each. None measures the count needed for fixed acceptance, and none covers a context made of the model's own reasoning.
ranked.outcome_a: Count saturates: draft attention cost per token is constant in context length, the ratio should shrink as 1/N instead of staying at 5%, and self-speculation's attention saving approaches the verification-amortisation limit (about 13x rather than 6.78x in SparseSpec's own example). Per-request draft memory is then a constant, which simplifies batch scheduling.
ranked.outcome_b: Count grows in proportion for reasoning traces: 5% is intrinsic there, the gain of sparse self-speculation on reasoning models does not grow with trace length, and going further needs something other than top-K selection (merged or summarised KV, a hierarchy of drafts as in TriForce).
ranked.design_it_points_to: A fixed-count budget policy with length-independent draft cost, or a hierarchical / merged-KV draft for reasoning traces. It also sets the asymptotic speedup one can claim for sparse self-speculation.
ranked.first_experiment: Same offline replay harness as card 1. Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Family (i), prompt length: PG-19 and LongBench items truncated to 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K, 64K with 256 generated tokens. Family (ii), generated length: AIME / LiveCodeBench reasoning traces with short prompts, measured at trace positions 1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K. For each point find K*, the smallest count at which per-token greedy agreement >= 0.95 and mean TV <= 0.05, for oracle top-K and for previous-step top-K. Fit K* ~ N^β per family and per layer. Decide A if β < 0.3 in both families; decide B for reasoning if β > 0.7 in family (ii). Stop if K* at the smallest N already exceeds 25% of the context in family (ii): the draft is not sparse there and the question is moot.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near D1 (decode-time KV page selection) in subject. Difference: D1 was an engine-level saving from fetching fewer pages; this is an offline scaling law for acceptance that bounds the gain of self-speculation. Not a 'does the gain survive condition C' question: it asks which law holds.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict sublinear growth in both families (exponent roughly 0.3-0.7) with reasoning traces higher than prompts; the direction is guessable, the exponent is not. Most experts would lean the same way with real doubt on the reasoning-trace case.
reasons.generative: A gives a fixed-count budget policy, which is close to a settings change with a better asymptote; B says top-K is bounded and gestures at merged or hierarchical KV without specifying it. Mostly a scaling law that bounds a claim.
reasons.reviewer: A K* ~ N^beta law for fixed acceptance, split by prompt versus self-generated context, is a real missing limit. It is a measurement more than a method, and the expert guess (constant for prompts, proportional for reasoning) is plausible enough to be unsurprising.
reasons.feasible: Only sampled positions need the K* search, so compute is modest, and 64K contexts fit in 48 GB on Llama-3.1-8B. Qwen3-8B's native window stops short of 64K, 16K reasoning traces must be collected first, and it needs the F05-style replay code.

ranked.question: Across attention heads, is sensitivity to key and value quantization the same property as sensitivity to token eviction, or the opposite one?

evidence.claim: Only sparse heads are robust to low-bit KV.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Lemma 1. Only attention heads with sparse and concentrated patterns demonstrate consistent robustness to low-precision KV cache quantization."

evidence.claim: Dispersed heads are the ones that need a large eviction budget.
evidence.quote_or_number: "most heads retain nearly all attention weights with a small cache (e.g., top 5%), while dispersed heads require larger cache proportions"

evidence.claim: Tolerance to low precision and tolerance to removal can come apart.
evidence.quote_or_number: "useful interactions differ in their precision requirements: some tolerate low-precision scores while remaining sensitive to removal"

evidence.claim: Key-quantization failures concentrate where attention is low-entropy, i.e. in sparse heads.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Matched Pythia checkpoints localize the main anomaly to a small-model low-entropy route-flip boundary."

evidence.claim: Head-level eviction allocators degrade more than uniform ones at 2 bits (confounded by a different quantizer).
evidence.quote_or_number: "when precision is reduced to as low as 2-bit, these methods experience a more pronounced performance degradation compared to KV pruning methods compatible with KIVI, such as SnapKV and PyramidKV"

evidence.claim: The joint allocation of tokens and bits is not predicted by local error, and a joint rate-distortion allocator loses to a simple rule.
evidence.quote_or_number: "keeping more tokens at low precision beats eviction alone in 17 of 18 settings"; "The best bit-width depends on the model and budget, and the offline attention error we measured does not predict it reliably"; "a joint rate-distortion allocator (RDKV) is 1.0 point less accurate"

evidence.claim: Eviction-relevant head importance moves within one input, while quantization sensitivity is said to be a fixed model property.
evidence.quote_or_number: PeekKV: "the signal at the last prefill token (prefill@last) attains an average rank correlation of only 0.58 with the reference ranking, whereas the signal at the first decode token (decode@1) ... reaches 0.77". KVTuner: "the sensitivity of LLMs and intermediate layers to KV cache quantization is the model property and independent of input prompts"

ranked.expert_prediction: Complementary. Diffuse heads average out zero-mean value noise but lose attention mass under eviction; sparse heads survive eviction but a key error can flip which token they select. So the heads that tolerate quantization are the ones that do not tolerate eviction.
ranked.why_uncertain: KVTuner's published lemma says the opposite (sparse heads are the robust ones under quantization), which together with Ada-KV would make diffuse heads fragile to both. Key and value sensitivity may have opposite signs with respect to head entropy, and KVTuner measures relative attention-output error, not downstream effect. No paper found puts the two per-head sensitivities side by side.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: abs:"KV cache" AND abs:quantization AND abs:eviction (25 results scanned); abs:"KV cache" AND abs:quantization AND abs:heads (25 scanned); all:"KV cache" AND quantization AND eviction AND ("per-head" OR "head-level" OR "head-wise"). WebSearch: per-head quantization sensitivity versus eviction sensitivity. Semantic Scholar citation lookups for KVTuner and AsymKV failed (rate limit).
ranked.closest_existing_answer: TriAttention (2611.07256) ranks per-layer, per-head sensitivity separately for 4-bit and for skipping but does not compare the two rankings. RateQuant (2605.06675, abstract) allocates bits per head only. ARKV (2603.08727, seen only in a search summary, not verified) assigns tokens to full, quantized or evicted tiers from layer-level statistics, not per head.
ranked.outcome_a: Same heads fragile to both: the two savings overlap and the diffuse heads bound both. One sensitivity score serves both allocators; head-level eviction budgets and low bit widths should not be stacked naively, and the combined gain is less than the product.
ranked.outcome_b: Opposite heads: choose the compression family per head. Evict in sparse heads at full precision, keep every token at 1-2 bits in diffuse heads. The gains multiply, and it needs a per-head-group page layout in the serving kernel (vLLM / FlashInfer).
ranked.design_it_points_to: A per-head choice between eviction and low-bit storage, or a single shared sensitivity score for joint token-and-bit allocation.
ranked.first_experiment: Models: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B, then Qwen3.5-9B. Data: 50 prompts (RULER 8K, a LongBench subset, teacher-forced reasoning traces). For every KV head apply four single-head interventions: keys to 2 bits, values to 2 bits, keep the top 10% of tokens by that head's attention, keep a random 10%. Record next-token KL against the unmodified model. Report Spearman correlation across heads between eviction KL and each quantization KL, regress each on head entropy, and check stability across prompts and between prefill and decode positions. Stop if a published table already shows this, or if all correlations are within plus or minus 0.2 on every model (then head-level structure does not justify a design).
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Uses head entropy like earlier residue (b) / Q23, but asks whether two sensitivities coincide across heads, not whether hybrid attention is more diffuse. Not D1: no decode-time page selection.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict a positive correlation dominated by plain head importance (important heads are fragile to any intervention), with the entropy-conditional sign unclear. KVTuner's lemma and the averaging argument do point in opposite directions, so there is real doubt after importance is factored out.
reasons.generative: B gives a per-head choice between eviction and low-bit storage with a kernel page layout consequence; A mostly says the gains do not stack and one score serves both, which is a caution more than a method.
reasons.reviewer: The KVTuner-versus-Ada-KV sign disagreement is a fair hook, but query 3 shows multi-axis allocation is crowded (MoE-nD 2604.17695 routes eviction/quantization/low-rank per layer, DiffKV, TriAttention). Per-head family choice is an incremental refinement with a hard kernel layout cost.
reasons.feasible: Single-head interventions with teacher-forced KL are simple, but about 256 KV heads x 4 interventions x 50 prompts of 8K is tens of thousands of forwards per model. That is about a GPU-day per model with prefix reuse, and single-head effects may be small.

ranked.question: When layers are removed from a model (depth pruning or layer skipping), does the 4-bit weight error that reaches the output grow because the removed layers were absorbing it, or shrink because there is less depth for it to accumulate over?

evidence.claim: One paper says pretrained blocks actively cancel inherited quantization error, most strongly in the middle blocks, and that this cancellation is a response to error at the block input, not something specific to the block's own quantized weights. It did not test layer removal.
evidence.source: arXiv 2609.11716, Why Does Post-Training Quantization Work? (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Counteraction offsets part of the newly introduced error, and slows the hidden-error norm growth." Qwen3-32B: removing counteraction raises final relative hidden error 2.94x; strongest in blocks 17-48; input-error response accounts for 99.9% of the negative interaction.

evidence.claim: A second paper says cross-layer cancellation is not what sets how much weight noise a network tolerates, and that deeper GPT-2 models tolerate more noise.
evidence.source: arXiv 2609.32060, Depth Laws for the Precision Floor of Trained Neural Networks (abstract and full text; the section with the cancellation test was past the part I could read)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Decision margins, cross-layer error cancellation and heavy tails do not set the floor." / "We test this mechanism in our networks and do not find it." / "Deeper GPT-2 models are more robust to perturbation"

evidence.claim: A pipeline paper claims depth pruning makes quantization more robust because the error path is shorter. The supporting numbers are near-ties.
evidence.source: arXiv 2608.30076, Budget-Aware Compression Pipeline for Single-GPU LLM Inference (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Controlled ablations show that layer-wise pruning makes weight quantization more robust." / "subsequent depth pruning shortens the path over which quantization errors accumulate and propagate." Table 5: Short-20 ARC-E 0.7222 vs AWQ-20 0.7205.

evidence.claim: The original layer-removal paper states the two savings are independent, without a measurement of the interaction.
evidence.quote_or_number: "ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods"

evidence.claim: The compression-order paper measures a large order effect for block removal plus 4-bit quantization but assumes layer-wise independence and has no analysis of which layers carry the interaction.
evidence.source: arXiv 2603.18426, Prune-then-Quantize or Quantize-then-Prune? (full text, first 100k characters)
evidence.quote_or_number: "introduce the Progressive Intensity Hypothesis, which states that weaker perturbations should precede stronger ones." Table 1 order advantage of quantize-then-prune, SLEB 5% with 4-bit QuaRot: -9.379; at 5-bit: -0.057.

evidence.claim: The user's own depth-pruned then AWQ-quantized models collapsed on instruction following while the unpruned AWQ model was fine. There was no healing before AWQ, so the cause is not separated.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Source AWQ: IFEval 0.855"; "All depth-pruned AWQ variants: IFEval 0.05–0.20"

evidence.claim: Over pretraining the two kinds of spare capacity may move in opposite directions: cancellation of quantization error grows with training, while early-exit potential is reported to shrink in newer models (the second claim is weakly supported by its own numbers).
evidence.source: arXiv 2609.11716 (full text) and arXiv 2603.23701, The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: 2609.11716: "counteraction is weak near initialization and becomes more pronounced at later checkpoints." 2603.23701: "Our results show a diminishing trend in early-exit effectiveness across newer model generations." EAS: Llama2-7B 0.52, Llama3-8B 0.46, Qwen2-7B 0.36, Qwen3-8B 0.51.

ranked.expert_prediction: Roughly additive at 4 bits when 25% or fewer layers are removed and the model is healed, with a mild extra penalty because the layers that similarity scores call removable (late-middle) sit in the same depth range where cancellation is strongest.
ranked.why_uncertain: Three published positions disagree: independent (ShortGPT), pruning helps quantization (2608.30076), and a mechanism that implies pruning should hurt it (2609.11716). A fourth paper says the cancellation mechanism does not set noise tolerance at all (2609.32060). None of them removed layers and re-measured quantization error growth, and the one concrete data point at hand (the user's run) is a collapse, not a mild penalty.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: "depth pruning then quantization LLM quantization error layers redundant block influence counteraction compensation joint layer pruning quantization interaction 2026"; WebSearch: "quantized LLM early exit OR layer skipping interaction ... error correction later layers ... 4-bit 2026". Semantic Scholar citations of 2609.11716 (one citing paper, 2609.32060), 2603.18426 (six, none on which layers carry the interaction), 2403.03853 and 2403.17887. Semantic Scholar keyword search and arXiv API search were rate-limited and returned nothing usable.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: arXiv 2603.18426 (order of pruning and quantization, including block removal with SLEB, but no per-layer mechanism) and arXiv 2510.23766 BitSkip (quantization and early exit compose poorly, on 85M models trained from scratch). Neither says whether the removable layers are the error-absorbing ones.
ranked.outcome_a: Absorber: removing high-cancellation blocks raises downstream quantization error more than removing blocks with the same similarity score but low cancellation. Then pruning and quantization spend the same spare capacity. One builds a layer-selection score computed on the quantized model with a cancellation term, or keeps the blocks after a cut at higher precision; a layer-skip draft of a 4-bit target has to exit later than one of a full-precision target.
ranked.outcome_b: Accumulator or neutral: quantization error at the output is unchanged or lower after removal. Then the two savings stack, the user's collapse is a calibration or interface problem (AWQ scale search on shifted activations, no healing), and the fix is to heal first and calibrate after. Layer skip on top of 4-bit weights becomes a reasonable self-draft.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A quantization-aware rule for which layers to prune or skip (or a precision map that depends on which layers were cut), versus treating depth and bit-width as independent knobs.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B and Qwen3.5-4B, 4-bit RTN (group 128) and GPTQ, forward passes only on 256 sequences (C4 plus model-generated reasoning traces). Per block, measure the ShortGPT Block Influence score and the counteraction cosine (inherited hidden error vs the block's own update error). Then remove k = 2, 4, 8 blocks chosen three ways: most removable by Block Influence, highest cancellation, lowest cancellation at matched Block Influence. For each, measure final relative hidden error of quantized vs full precision on the cut network, output total variation, and the 2x2 interaction (cut x quantize) on total variation and on GSM8K (300 items) and IFEval. Stop if the interaction is within 10% of additive for every selection and the rank correlation between Block Influence and cancellation across blocks is below 0.2 in absolute value: then there is nothing to build.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: none of D1-D4. A sibling harvest (composition and theory) dropped "depth pruning x quantization" as predictable sub-additivity; this card differs by naming the mechanism in dispute and the published disagreement. Not in the earlier 35 questions.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict roughly additive to mildly superadditive interaction, with the cancellation-based selection arms differing only slightly. Three published positions disagree and the absorber mechanism has not been tested by removal, so the lean is weak.
reasons.generative: A gives a quantization-aware layer-selection score with a cancellation term or a post-cut precision map; B reduces to a procedure fix (heal first, calibrate after) and treating the knobs as independent.
reasons.reviewer: The absorber-versus-accumulator disagreement is specific and the experiment is cheap. Pruning-times-quantization composition is a crowded area, and a quantization-aware layer score is an incremental contribution.
reasons.feasible: Forward-only measurements with RTN/GPTQ and block removal on 256 sequences plus small GSM8K and IFEval runs fit comfortably in a week. The matched-Block-Influence selection may not exist if the two scores are correlated, and a clean answer for the healed case needs fine-tuning.

ranked.question: Why do hybrid models keep their quality with 50x to 250x oracle top-k attention when their attention mass is more spread out than in pure transformers: is the mass that top-k drops redundant with what the recurrent layers already carry, and what quantity predicts how many tokens a layer needs?

evidence.claim: Published: hybrids tolerate far higher context sparsity than pure transformers.
evidence.quote_or_number: hybrid architectures such as Qwen3.5 and Gemma3 exhibit significantly greater robustness to context sparsity, maintaining performance even at up to 50x sparsity with little to no degradation in quality

evidence.claim: Down to 128 retrieved tokens.
evidence.quote_or_number: restricting attention to just 128 retrieved tokens corresponds to approximately 250x sparsity while still preserving strong performance

evidence.claim: The paper offers a guess, not a test, for the cause.
evidence.quote_or_number: suggesting that the inclusion of SSM or linear-attention layers may inherently improve resilience to sparse context retrieval

evidence.claim: The result uses exact oracle top-k, the same selection rule as the user's measurement.
evidence.quote_or_number: The primary mechanism is exact oracle top-k selection (to eliminate confounds from approximate top-k indexers)

evidence.claim: The user measured the opposite sign on attention mass: top-512 misses twice as much mass on the hybrid.
evidence.quote_or_number: H-a REFUTED (oracle@512 misses 22.7% on Qwen3.5 vs 11.6% Qwen3-4B; every layer more diffuse)

evidence.claim: The paper's own 5x setting shows output error much smaller than the density would suggest, i.e. mass and output error are different quantities.
evidence.quote_or_number: Sink(128) + Local(128) + OracleTopK with heavy fraction 0.20 (achieved density ~22%; per-layer attention-output L2 error ~1.3% relative to full attention)

evidence.claim: A 2026 preprint adds a linear-attention summary of the unretrieved tokens to top-k attention, which is the same idea built by hand. Seen only in a search snippet.
evidence.source: Top-K Retrieval with Fixed-Size Linear-Attention Completion, arXiv 2604.05438 (not read)
evidence.quote_or_number: snippet only; no quote taken

ranked.expert_prediction: Both observations are true and the link between them is that missed mass is the wrong predictor. In a hybrid the attention layers are few and act as a retrieval path, the dropped tail carries near-average value vectors whose contribution the recurrent layers already supply, so output error stays small while mass coverage looks poor.
ranked.why_uncertain: Three other readings fit: (1) normalisation, the residue (b) from the prior search: hybrids have fewer attention layers and different head counts, so 'mass missed at 512' is not comparable across the two models; (2) the paper's benchmarks (RULER, AIME, LOFT, SWE) are needle-like and do not need the diffuse tail, while the user's prompts did; (3) model size, since the paper's strongest claims are for Qwen3.5-27B and the user measured 4B. If (2) or (3) holds, the tolerance is not a property of the architecture and the kernel consequence disappears.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: 'why hybrid SSM attention models robust to sparse top-k attention Qwen3.5 Gemma3 linear attention completion'. Read 2605.24168 in full sections; snippets for 2604.05438 and HyLRA 2602.00777 (both unverified); the user's verification.md residue (b).
ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2605.24168 reports the tolerance and guesses at the cause without a test. 2604.05438 (snippet only) builds a linear-attention completion for pure transformers, which supports the redundancy reading but does not analyse Qwen3.5 or Gemma3.
ranked.outcome_a: Dropped mass is redundant with the recurrent state: then the right selection signal is output sensitivity given the state, not attention mass, hybrids need only 16 to 128 tokens per layer, and their attention sits in the short-list regime of the previous card, where the kernel floor, not bytes, sets speed. One builds a state-conditioned selector and a short-list kernel for hybrids.
ranked.outcome_b: The tolerance is a benchmark or size effect and the 4B hybrid really needs the diffuse tail: then sparse attention is a worse fit for small hybrids than for transformers, the published robustness claim needs a stated limit, and one stops building sparse decode for hybrids on 48 GB cards.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A predictor of tokens needed per layer (output-error based, conditioned on recurrent state) and, if tolerance holds, a decode path for hybrids with a fixed tiny attention budget.
ranked.first_experiment: One 48 GB card, Qwen3.5-4B (hybrid) and Qwen3-4B, teacher-forced on the same long prompts the user used for H-a plus one RULER-style set. Per attention layer and K in {32, 128, 512}: (i) attention mass missed by oracle top-K, (ii) relative L2 error of the attention output, (iii) KL of the final logits when all layers use top-K. Then one intervention on the hybrid: replace the dropped tail by its mean value vector, and separately reset the recurrent state 2K tokens back, and see which one changes (iii). Stop if at K=128 the hybrid's final-logit KL is not lower than the transformer's on both prompt sets; then the published tolerance does not hold at 4B and the answer is outcome B with a size or benchmark limit to report.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Builds on residue (b) of the prior search (is hybrid attention really more diffuse or a normalisation artifact) and is near D1 (selection). It differs from residue (b) by asking why the published tolerance and the measured spread can both hold, and from D1 by not proposing a page selector; D2 (state checkpoints) is not involved.

reasons.unpredictable: I lean toward the tolerance being largely an oracle-top-k plus needle-like-benchmark effect (dense models also tolerate oracle top-k), with some real redundancy, at about 60%. The user's own online ratio of 1.03 supports that lean, but the redundancy reading is not ruled out.
reasons.generative: A gives a state-conditioned selector and a fixed tiny-budget decode path for hybrids; B is a stated limit on a published claim and a decision to stop building sparse decode for small hybrids.
reasons.reviewer: Why hybrids tolerate extreme top-k despite diffuse attention is a real contradiction with a state-conditioned selector as payoff. Benchmark and model-size confounds may dissolve it, and it leans on killed D1 measurements.
reasons.feasible: Oracle top-K per attention layer, the tail-mean substitution and the state reset on 4B models are teacher-forced and fit one card. They need custom access to attention internals and GDN state, and the published claim is strongest at 27B, which is awkward to hook in PyTorch on 48 GB.

ranked.question: What determines whether a model's KV-cache error budget sits in the keys or in the values (attention sink, key normalisation, the attention output gate, or projection norms), and does one offline statistic predict it across dense, gated-hybrid and diffusion models?

evidence.claim: KV quantization theory says keys always deserve more bits.
evidence.quote_or_number: "key projections systematically have larger spectral and Frobenius norms than value matrices"; "for any given memory budget, prioritizing precision for keys over values strictly reduces quantization error"; "key-favored allocations (e.g., 4-bit keys, 2-bit values) retain up to 98.3% accuracy"

evidence.claim: Two more papers state the key-over-value rule; one names Qwen2.5-7B as the sensitive model.
evidence.quote_or_number: AsymKV: "the transformer's output loss is more sensitive to the quantization of key matrices". KVTuner: "why key cache is generally more important than value cache for quantization error reduction"; "4.0-bit for sensitive models like Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct".

evidence.claim: On gated hybrids the useful signal is in the values, and the value-to-key dispersion ratio differs by 4x across families; the paper reports a correlation with sink strength but no mechanism, and two models do not fit a pure sink story.
evidence.quote_or_number: σV/σK: Llama-3.1-8B 0.33, Llama-3.2-3B 0.40, Qwen3-4B (QK-norm, sink rate 0.548) 0.97, Qwen2.5-3B 1.19, Qwen2.5-7B 1.34, Qwen3.5-4B (gated, sink rate 0.015) 1.36, Qwen3.5-9B 1.49, GPT-OSS-20B 1.67. BOS mass: Llama-3.1-8B 0.591, Qwen3-4B 0.408, Qwen3.5-4B 0.034. "weaker sinks co-occur with greater value-vector dispersion relative to key-vector dispersion". MATH-500 at 25% budget on Qwen3.5-4B: ValueDiff 84.3, KeyDiff 65.2, TOVA 39.3, SnapKV 24.7.

evidence.claim: A cache-fill study finds the error in keys on Llama and in values plus recurrent state on Qwen3.5, with Qwen3 needing both.
evidence.source: RidgeFill (arXiv 2611.09709), abstract and introduction (splice tables in the unread tail)
evidence.quote_or_number: error is in "the keys on Llama-3.1-8B, half of it in their scale" and in "the values and the recurrent state on Qwen3.5-9B"; Qwen models "normalize their keys, which fixes each key's size"; key rescale at split 12 halves added loss from +1.006 to +0.502 nats.

evidence.claim: Per-layer structure exists: some layers are key-dominated, some value-dominated, and in some more precision hurts.
evidence.quote_or_number: "K-dominated versus V-dominated layers and negative-transfer layers where increased precision degrades quality"

evidence.claim: The attention output gate scales the value path by a layer-dependent factor that spans more than 10x.
evidence.quote_or_number: budget per layer is set by "the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers"

evidence.claim: For diffusion LMs the key-first claim is asserted for cache reuse without a key-only vs value-only measurement.
evidence.quote_or_number: "K quantization can therefore redirect attention across reused and recomputed positions"; "reducing quantization error alone may fail to predict generation quality"

ranked.expert_prediction: Key sensitivity follows the sink: models with a strong sink are key-sensitive, sink-suppressed models are value-sensitive, and σV/σK ranks them.
ranked.why_uncertain: Qwen2.5 has no sink-suppression mechanism yet a value-heavy ratio (1.19-1.34) and is the sensitive model in KVTuner; Qwen3-4B has a clear sink (BOS mass 0.408, sink rate 0.548) yet ratio 0.97 and RidgeFill says Qwen3-8B needs both sides. So key normalisation or the output gate may be the real variable. Also, a dispersion ratio measured for eviction need not predict damage under quantization or low rank; nobody has run key-only vs value-only perturbation on gated hybrids or diffusion LMs.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search "key value cache quantization keys values sensitivity asymmetric" (2 results: AsymKV, TurboAngle). WebSearch on why keys are more sensitive than values and whether that holds without a sink, with QK-norm or gated attention (found 2502.15075, KVTuner, and a 2609.19880 snippet not checked by id). Read ValueDiff body and RidgeFill intro for a quantization or low-rank K/V split on hybrids: none.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: ValueDiff 2609.23314 (eviction scores only, correlation without mechanism) and RidgeFill 2611.09709 (cache-fill splices on three models). Neither covers quantization or low rank, and neither isolates sink vs key-norm vs gate.
ranked.outcome_a: One offline statistic (σV/σK, or gate mean times value norm) ranks all models: a rule for splitting bits or rank between keys and values on any new model before running it, including gate-aware value precision per layer on hybrids and a Palu-style rank split.
ranked.outcome_b: No model-level statistic predicts it: allocation has to be per layer, the key-first theorems describe two model families rather than attention in general, and published key-heavy defaults should not be carried to hybrids or diffusion LMs without a per-layer probe.
ranked.design_it_points_to: An architecture-aware K/V allocation rule for KV quantization and low-rank compression (bits and rank), set from a cheap offline probe, with the gate as a per-layer weight on value precision in gated hybrids.
ranked.first_experiment: Teacher-forced on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B, LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B: perturb keys only or values only (8, 4, 2 bits; low rank at matched bytes), per layer and all layers, and measure NLL change (denoising loss for the diffusion models). Regress the key-to-value damage ratio on σV/σK, sink rate, spectral-norm ratio of the projections, a key-norm flag and mean gate. Stop if σV/σK alone already ranks all models with Spearman 0.9 or more; then the answer is in ValueDiff's table and only the rule is missing.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Not D1-D4. Near the sibling KV-compression card on whether low-bit damage is bias or error size for keys vs values; this one asks which architectural property sets the split and adds hybrids and diffusion LMs. Near residue (b) through the sink.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict no single model-level statistic ranks all eight models and that allocation ends up per layer; 'one statistic predicts it' questions usually resolve to 'partially'. The Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 counterexamples to the sink story leave real doubt about which variable matters.
reasons.generative: A gives an architecture-aware K/V bit-and-rank split rule from a cheap probe, useful for Palu-style methods but close to an allocation setting; B says allocation must be per layer and published defaults do not transfer, a caution.
reasons.reviewer: What sets the key/value error split is a fair contradiction (Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 break the sink story) with an allocation-rule payoff relevant to Palu. The eight-model sweep including diffusion LMs is diffuse, and ValueDiff and RidgeFill are close.
reasons.feasible: Key-only and value-only perturbations with NLL readout are easy on the six autoregressive models. The two diffusion LMs add separate codebases and a different loss, and a regression across eight models is weak, but the first signal arrives within a week.

ranked.question: In gated-attention hybrids, did the no-op that dense models express as attention to the sink move into the output gate, so that the heads and steps where attention looks diffuse are the ones whose gate is nearly closed and missing attention there is harmless?

evidence.claim: The gate is head-specific, query-dependent and sparse, and it removes the sink.
evidence.quote_or_number: "applying a head-specific sigmoid gate after the Scaled Dot-Product Attention"; "applying query-dependent sparse gating scores to modulate the SDPA output"; "this sparse gating mechanism mitigates 'attention sink'"

evidence.claim: Sink mass falls by more than 10x from the dense Qwen3 to the gated Qwen3.5.
evidence.quote_or_number: BOS attention mass: Qwen3-4B 0.408; Qwen3.5-4B 0.034; Qwen3.5-9B 0.031

evidence.claim: The gate's mean varies by more than 10x across layers and has only been used as a static per-layer budget.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the model's native attention output gate, whose mean differs by more than an order of magnitude across layers"

evidence.claim: Own data: the hybrid misses about twice the attention mass at the same budget, yet moves its output 7.4-7.5x less per unit of missing mass offline; minimum missing attention is not maximum accuracy.
evidence.source: kv-fetch EXPERIMENTS.md (own project) and earlier verification notes
evidence.quote_or_number: H1: oracle shared set at 512 misses 22.7% of attention on Qwen3.5-4B vs 11.6% on Qwen3-4B (about 23.5% vs 19.6% after removing the sink and renormalising, per verification.md); "7.4-7.5x lower KL over three pairs with matched missing attention (confounded: 8 perturbed layers vs 36)"; "minimum missing attention per step is not maximum accuracy"

ranked.expert_prediction: Partly yes: closed-gate heads account for a good share of the diffuse attention, and gate-weighted missing mass brings the hybrid close to the dense model's non-sink figure.
ranked.why_uncertain: The offline KL advantage did not help online (ratio 1.03), the 8-vs-36 perturbed-layer confound could explain the KL ratio on its own, and the gate might be a smooth per-dimension scale rather than a near on/off signal per head and step, in which case it carries no information about which missing mass matters. The renormalised gap (23.5% vs 19.6%) is already small, so the gate may have little left to explain.
ranked.prior_answer_search: No dedicated web search was run for this card (search budget went to the other four). Checked the 2505.06708 abstract, the GateSight body (gate used only as a per-layer mean), the ValueDiff body (no gate analysis), and the repo's verification notes on residue (b). arXiv API keyword search was rate-limited. A per-step, per-head analysis of gate value against attention entropy or sparse-attention error was not found in anything read.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: Gated Attention 2505.06708 (shows the sink goes away and the gate is sparse, on its own training runs, with no link to sparse-attention or eviction error) and GateSight 2610.14754 (uses the layer-mean gate as a budget).
ranked.outcome_a: Yes: coverage targets and KV selectors on gated hybrids should weight missing mass by the gate, the D1 coverage ceiling was measured with the wrong weight, and at long context a head whose gate is closed can skip its KV read, since the gate is computed from the query before attention.
ranked.outcome_b: No: the diffuseness is real attention that matters, selection and eviction on gated models have a floor that dense-model results hide behind the sink, and the lower offline KL is a layer-count effect.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Gate-weighted coverage as the error metric for any sparse or evicted KV method on Qwen3.5-class models, and gate-predicted skipping of attention reads per head and step as a long-context kernel saving.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3.5-4B on the existing teacher-forced traces, plus Qwen3-4B as the dense reference. Per head and step record gate magnitude, attention entropy, oracle@512 missing mass and the logit effect of the sparse approximation. Test whether (a) diffuse steps are closed-gate steps, (b) gate-weighted missing mass predicts per-step KL better than raw missing mass, (c) the KL-per-missing-mass ratio against Qwen3-4B moves toward 1 after gate weighting and after matching the number of perturbed layers. Stop if gate magnitude and attention entropy correlate below 0.2 in every layer. The gate's exact form in Qwen3.5 (per head or per dimension) must be read from the model code first; it was taken from the abstract and config flag only.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Builds directly on residue (b) and on D1's measurements; near earlier Q23 and the sibling composition-theory card on whether hybrid attention layers are in a different key-query regime once the sink is removed. Differs by naming the gate as the per-step weight. It does not revive D1: the gate is per step and head, not per token, so it gives no eviction rule.

reasons.unpredictable: I lean 'partly yes': the gate is likely a smooth per-dimension scale that correlates modestly with diffuse steps but explains little of the already small renormalised gap. The gate's actual form in Qwen3.5 is unverified, so the lean is soft.
reasons.generative: A gives gate-weighted coverage as the error metric and gate-predicted skipping of KV reads per head and step, a real kernel saving; B establishes a floor and attributes the KL advantage to layer count, ending the work.
reasons.reviewer: Gate-weighted coverage and gate-predicted KV-read skipping are concrete and cheap to test. The hypothesis is natural given the Gated Attention paper, the renormalised gap left to explain is small, and the gate may be per-dimension and uninformative.
reasons.feasible: The measurement is one GPU-day of logging per head and step on 4B models. Whether it can run as designed depends on the form of the gate in the Qwen3.5 code (per head or per dimension), which is not yet checked.

ranked.question: When an approximate or low-bit KV cache changes a diffusion LM's accuracy under confidence-threshold decoding, is that because the representations are wrong or because the cache changes which tokens get committed at which step?

evidence.claim: The KV quantization paper for diffusion LMs decodes with a confidence threshold, reports no step counts, runs each setting once, and says error size may not predict quality.
evidence.quote_or_number: "confidence-threshold parallel decoding with threshold 0.9"; "single-run inference evaluations under fixed decoding and quantization settings, not averages over random seeds"; "reducing quantization error alone may fail to predict generation quality"; "Runtime, throughput, and peak-memory measurements are outside the current experimental claims"

evidence.claim: Accuracy moves in both directions under caching alone, and 4-bit caches sometimes beat the unquantized cache.
evidence.quote_or_number: LLaDA full attention / prefix cache / dual cache: HumanEval 42.07 / 42.07 / 35.98, MBPP 29.80 / 26.60 / 25.80. Dream: HumanEval 39.63 / 43.29 / 37.20. 4-bit vs cache-only: LLaDA dual GSM8K 78.62 vs 77.94, MBPP 26.80 vs 25.80; Dream prefix MBPP 56.20 vs 55.20.

evidence.claim: The original approximate-cache paper also shows gains and losses from the cache, gives step counts by threshold only, and supports cache closeness with a qualitative similarity plot.
evidence.quote_or_number: Baseline to +Cache at length 256: Dream HumanEval 49.4 to 53.7, MBPP 56.6 to 53.2, MATH 38.4 to 36.8; LLaDA HumanEval 41.5 to 42.7. NFE 9 / 12 / 20 at thresholds 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 on one prompt. Refresh interval 2 / 8 / 32 on LLaDA-V MathVista: 59.2% / 58.2% / 56.6%. Similarity described as "consistently close to 1".

evidence.claim: Another cache paper states that its cache choice changes the generation order and improves quality.
evidence.quote_or_number: its cache "can enable quasi left-to-right generation and mitigate premature overconfidence in tokens at the end of the sequence" and "yields consistent improvements in generation quality"

evidence.claim: In recurrent hybrids, a small biased per-step error changed how long generation runs, not per-step quality; a stale cache is also a biased view.
evidence.quote_or_number: "so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution"

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly small representation noise: step counts and commit order move by a few percent, 4-bit sits under the staleness floor, and much of the up-and-down in the tables is single-run noise (HumanEval has 164 problems).
ranked.why_uncertain: A stale cache is not zero-mean noise: it shows a more-masked context than the current one, which should shift confidence in one direction, and a threshold rule turns a confidence shift into a different commit schedule. The size of the swings (Dream HumanEval +4.3 with cache, LLaDA HumanEval -6.1 with dual cache) is large for a cache described as nearly identical, and d2Cache openly attributes its quality gain to a changed order. No paper reports steps or commit order per cache setting, so the two channels have never been separated.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search "diffusion language model KV cache staleness error quantization" (0 results). WebSearch on diffusion LM approximate KV cache error, confidence-threshold decoding and number of function evaluations (found Fast-dLLM 2505.22618, d2Cache 2509.23094, LaCache 2607.16339). Read Fast-dLLM and dLLM-KVQ bodies for NFE per cache setting, seed variance, or a forced-schedule replay: none.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: dLLM-KVQ 2610.39853 (writes total error as reuse error plus quantization error but measures neither the interaction nor the decoding trajectory) and d2Cache 2509.23094 (claims an order effect for its own method, abstract only).
ranked.outcome_a: Schedule channel dominates: report steps and commit order beside every cache or quantization result; recalibrate the confidence threshold together with cache age and bit width; expect lower bit widths and longer refresh intervals to work once the commit rule is corrected; some published cache 'quality gains' are a different decoding order that could be had without the cache.
ranked.outcome_b: Representation channel dominates: bits and refresh interval are the levers and should be set together against a shared error budget; the commit rule can be left alone and cache comparisons across papers are fair at equal threshold.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a cache-aware commit rule (threshold as a function of cache age and precision) or an age-scheduled bit allocation for diffusion-LM KV caches, plus a reporting standard (steps, commit order, seeds) for dLLM cache papers.
ranked.first_experiment: LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B with the public Fast-dLLM code, GSM8K and a 500-problem MATH subset plus HumanEval, 3 seeds: full recomputation, prefix cache, dual cache, each with and without 4-bit and 2-bit cache quantization. Log tokens committed per step, their positions and confidences, and total steps. Then replay each cached run under the full-recomputation commit schedule, and the reverse, to separate the two channels. Stop if step counts and commit order differ by under 2% across settings and schedule replay changes accuracy by less than the seed spread.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: None with D1-D4. Related in spirit to residue (a): it asks whether a per-step error acts through the generation trajectory rather than through per-step quality, in a model family the earlier search did not cover. Weakest of the five: the expert guess (noise) may simply be right.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict the large table swings are mostly single-run noise (164 problems), but that a stale cache does shift confidence one way and changes the commit schedule measurably. Most would lean 'noise plus small schedule effect'; the split between channels is uncertain.
reasons.generative: A gives a cache-aware commit rule for diffusion LMs; B is joint tuning of bits and refresh interval against an error budget, a settings recommendation. The likely outcome (noise) produces only a reporting standard.
reasons.reviewer: Separating schedule and representation channels by replaying commit schedules is a good design and dLLM caching is active. d2Cache already claims an order effect, the noise explanation may simply hold, and it is far from the researcher's stack.
reasons.feasible: Fast-dLLM, LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B are public and fit one card. Adding cache quantization, commit logging and a schedule-replay mode to the decoding loop is a few days of work in a codebase outside the user's usual stack.

ranked.question: In a hybrid model, is an error made by an attention layer absorbed by the recurrent layers within a few hundred tokens, or written into the recurrent state where it persists?

evidence.claim: The user's hybrid shows much lower next-token KL per unit of missing attention than the dense model, yet no online advantage.
evidence.quote_or_number: "7.4-7.5x lower KL over three pairs with matched missing attention (confounded: 8 perturbed layers vs 36)"; "The offline KL advantage does not survive long generation."; at budget 512 Qwen3.5-4B 49.6% to 30.0%, Qwen3-4B 48.3% to 33.3%

evidence.claim: A quantization study reports that the Gated DeltaNet recurrence damps noise and forgets impulses quickly.
evidence.source: Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization, arXiv 2609.04098 (abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: "holds injected noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens"; "forgets a state impulse within hundreds of steps"

evidence.claim: A second study reports that a very small systematic error in the stored recurrent state makes hybrids reason longer.
evidence.quote_or_number: "With bf16 RTN state, five of six models reason longer."

evidence.claim: In Qwen3.5 the recurrent layers build the query that attention uses, so attention and recurrent state are coupled in both directions.
evidence.source: Who Asks, Who Answers, arXiv 2611.01909 (Abstract, Sec 4.1)
