Report conditional overlap against the independence baseline, overlap vs full-model entropy, and acceptance of (iii) vs the product of (i) and (ii). Stop if overlap equals the independence baseline and disagreement between (i) and (ii) predicts full-model mismatch no better than entropy alone.

reasons.unpredictable: Partial overlap well above independence, driven by shared low-margin positions, with stacked rejection between max(a,b) and the independence value; almost any expert would say this. Only the exact position between the two references is open.
reasons.generative: A gives a composite W4 plus sparse-KV self-draft that removes SparseSpec's short-context limit; B gives a two-draft disagreement trigger or a context-length router. Both are concrete, though the space is narrower than a new verification rule.
reasons.reviewer: Rejection overlap between sparse-KV and W4 drafts is unreported and the stacked draft is practical. A reviewer would see it as an incremental SparseSpec plus QuantSpec combination, with a fairly predictable entropy-driven overlap.
reasons.feasible: The W4 arm is a plain teacher-forced pass with a public AWQ copy and the overlap statistics are trivial. The sparse and stacked arms need the same custom two-stream replay as F05, and the 16-32K items need chunked attention capture.

ranked.question: When a compressed-KV self-drafter is stacked with a small or MTP drafter, are the two drafters rejected at the same tokens, at unrelated tokens, or at complementary tokens?

evidence.claim: The composed speedup VeriCache reports is an ideal figure, not a measured one.
evidence.quote_or_number: "VeriCache + Eagle reaches 4.35 × ideal speedup vs. 3.50 × for VeriCache alone and 1.78 × for Eagle alone (Appendix C)"

evidence.claim: That figure rests on an independence assumption, and the HTML shows no experimental support after it.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Under chain-independence of the two drafters, the expected accepted draft length per cycle becomes γ(x, c) · x · [1 + γ_e(d_e) · (d_e − 1)]"

evidence.claim: The two drafter kinds differ by an order of magnitude in accepted length, so they are not the same kind of predictor.
evidence.quote_or_number: "25–40 accepted tokens per verification round for VeriCache vs. only 2–3 for typical small-model drafters"

evidence.claim: Entropy predicts rejection of a sparse-KV self-drafter only weakly.
evidence.quote_or_number: "negative draft entropy obtains an acceptance AUC of 0.638 on RULER QA1. Tokens in the low-entropy bin are accepted at 86.3%, compared with 62.1% in the high-entropy bin."

evidence.claim: For MTP drafters, acceptance is said to follow entropy closely.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the MTP acceptance rate is fundamentally bounded by the fluctuation of model entropy, which demonstrates a clear negative linear relationship with the rise of entropy in the RL stage"

evidence.claim: Cascade analyses of self-drafters also assume how acceptance carries across levels instead of measuring it.
evidence.quote_or_number: "we assume c_d2 = 0.01 and α(M_t, M_d2) = α(M_d1, M_d2)"

ranked.expert_prediction: Positively correlated: both drafters fail where the target is uncertain. Under that guess the cascade does better than the independence formula, because a token the small drafter got right is an easy token where the compressed-KV pass is also right.
ranked.why_uncertain: The two failure modes may be different in kind. A small drafter fails where computation is hard. A compressed-KV drafter is the full model with missing context, so it can be confidently wrong at a low-entropy token whose supporting fact was dropped; the AUC of 0.638 above fits that reading. If so, the rejections are close to independent or even negatively related, and the sign of the correlation decides whether stacking beats or misses the published formula.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search: "speculative decoding" heterogeneous drafters; "speculative decoding" drafters "complementary" errors acceptance; "speculative decoding" correlated rejections cascade; "speculative decoding" "same tokens" rejected; "speculative decoding" "hard tokens" drafters. WebSearch: cascade SD two drafters rejection correlation independence assumption compressed KV drafter plus EAGLE. No paper found that measures token-level overlap of rejections between drafter families.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: MetaSD (2604.05417) chooses among several drafters with a bandit on alignment feedback, which implies drafters differ by domain, but it works at task level (abstract only read). HCSpec (ACL 2026, seen only in a web result) uses two draft modules in a horizontal cascade; I could not confirm how it models joint acceptance. TriForce and CAS-Spec stack levels without reporting overlap.
ranked.outcome_a: Rejections coincide (one difficulty axis). Then a cheap signal from the small drafter can tell the system when the compressed-KV pass is safe, the middle verification can be skipped on easy spans, and a single target-side quantity predicts the gain of both drafters.
ranked.outcome_b: Rejections are unrelated or complementary. Then the independence formula is right or optimistic, the compressed-KV drafter needs its own failure signal (missing attention mass, not entropy), and the better design is a two-branch draft: one branch from each drafter, since they cover different tokens.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a single-controller cascade (one confidence signal schedules both levels) or a two-branch drafter with a context-loss detector for the KV branch. It also fixes which draft-length controllers are worth building for sparse-KV drafters: entropy-based ones only make sense under outcome A.
ranked.first_experiment: Teacher-forced along the full model's greedy output. Target Qwen3-8B (and Llama-3.1-8B if a public EAGLE-3 or DFlash drafter is available for it). Drafter 1: the target with a sparse or compacted KV (top-K at 5% and a 4x compaction). Drafter 2: a public EAGLE-3 or DFlash checkpoint for the target, or Qwen3-1.7B as a plain small drafter. On about 100 reasoning traces and 50 long-context prompts, record per token: whether each drafter's top choice matches the target, target entropy and top-1 margin, and each drafter's own entropy. Report the phi correlation of the two rejection indicators, the same within entropy bins, and the composed accepted length three ways: replayed from the per-token records, the VeriCache independence formula, and full nesting. Stop if |phi| < 0.05 and the replayed length is within 5% of the independence formula on both workloads.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: None of D1 to D4. Earlier Q01/Q02 asked about SD break-even under batch load; this is about token-level structure of rejections and involves no load condition.

reasons.unpredictable: Positively correlated rejections (phi roughly 0.2-0.4) driven by target uncertainty, with a confident-wrong tail for the KV drafter; neither independence nor complementarity is plausible. Same predictable shape as F06 and F16.
reasons.generative: A gives a single-controller cascade where the small drafter's signal schedules the compressed-KV level; B gives a two-branch drafter with a context-loss detector. Both are concrete and also settle which draft-length controllers are worth building.
reasons.reviewer: The sign of rejection correlation between a compressed-KV drafter and a small drafter does decide cascade design, and the 'confidently wrong from missing context' reading is plausible. It is one measurement within a cascade paper, and MetaSD and HCSpec are nearby.
reasons.feasible: Per-token match records for a sparse-KV draft and Qwen3-1.7B or a public EAGLE-3/DFlash drafter are teacher-forced and cheap. The sparse replay and the 4x compaction drafter are the build items.

ranked.question: Do the extra reasoning tokens of a 4-bit model start at the same positions that cost it accuracy (confident symbolic tokens), or at the uncertain discourse positions where its output distribution differs most from full precision?

evidence.claim: A per-token routing experiment between the full-precision and 4-bit model attributes the accuracy loss to low-entropy positions. It did not report reasoning length per arm, and its low-entropy arm is about three quarters of all tokens.
evidence.quote_or_number: "τ=0.6, which corresponds to approximately the top 25% highest-entropy tokens."; "quantization-induced failures are dominated by errors at low-entropy token prediction, rather than high-entropy token prediction."

evidence.claim: The length paper locates the divergence at high-entropy positions and treats length with a penalty on hesitation markers; it did no routing experiment. Across model-quantizer pairs, length and accuracy move together.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Position-level KL divergence correlates strongly with the BF16 model's next-token entropy (Spearman ρ=0.92)."; "ρ = −0.73" across "28 model-quantization pairs"; the marker penalty cuts CoT length 12–23%.

evidence.claim: The low-entropy errors are sampling slips on digits and operators, not changes of the top token, and at very uncertain steps the quantized model becomes more concentrated, not less.
evidence.quote_or_number: "locally constrained symbolic decisions such as digits and operators."; "these errors are not driven by top-1 flips."; "the entropy shift becomes negative in high-uncertainty steps."

evidence.claim: Length can rise with accuracy essentially unchanged, which suggests the two failures can separate.
evidence.quote_or_number: Qwen3-30B GPTQ INT4: accuracy drop 0.2 points with average CTIR +3.7%.

evidence.claim: In the recurrent-state case most runs that never finish are exact repetition loops, which are low-entropy states, not hesitation at uncertain positions.
evidence.quote_or_number: 85% of unfinished bf16 runs on Qwen3.5-9B are exact repetition loops.

ranked.expert_prediction: Different positions: accuracy is lost at confident symbolic tokens, extra length starts at uncertain discourse positions, and fixing one does little for the other.
ranked.why_uncertain: The two papers each measured only their own outcome. ReQAT's low-entropy arm sends about 75% of tokens to full precision, so it does not show that those positions matter more per token. Length and accuracy are correlated at -0.73 across configurations, and a slipped digit is a plausible trigger for re-checking, in which case the hesitation markers are a symptom and the cause is at the symbolic positions.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: "quantized LLM selective full-precision verification only at low-entropy OR high-entropy tokens which token flips change final answer reasoning model token-level precision switching oracle replacement 2026". Semantic Scholar citations of 2606.00206. Read ReQAT, ReSET and 2606.00206 in full for a routing experiment that reports length: none.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: arXiv 2606.15682 ReQAT (entropy routing, accuracy only, W4A4KV4 formats) and arXiv 2602.02711 Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing (step-level routing in agent tasks, "only about 1% of the steps" are critical).
ranked.outcome_a: Same positions: sending only a narrow class of confident symbolic tokens (digits, operators) to full precision restores both accuracy and length. One builds a 4-bit decoder with full-precision re-scoring on that class, sharing the KV cache, and drops marker penalties as symptom treatment.
ranked.outcome_b: Different positions: length is a separate failure that a free decoding-time fix handles (marker penalty or temperature at uncertain steps), and precision routing is only worth its cost when accuracy is actually lost. Then 4-bit plus a penalty is the serving configuration for cases like GPTQ INT4 where accuracy is intact.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Where a mixed-precision decoder should spend its full-precision passes, and whether length inflation needs precision at all.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-4B full precision plus AWQ INT3 and INT4 copies in memory on one card, custom generation loop that picks per token which model's logits to sample from, using the full-precision entropy with the threshold at the top 25%. Arms: all 4-bit; all full precision; low-entropy to full precision; high-entropy to full precision; and two matched-count arms (a random 25% to full precision, the lowest-entropy 25% to full precision) so arms with equal token counts can be compared. 150 MATH-500 problems, same sampling noise across arms. Measure accuracy, reasoning length, cap hits. Stop if no arm moves length more than the random-25% arm does: length is then not tied to a position class, and the question reduces to the accumulated-error question in the previous card.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near the earlier compensation-vs-symptom question on extra tokens and earlier Q05; differs by using position-level replacement to locate the cause of length separately from the cause of accuracy loss. Sibling harvests ask which tokens do the damage for sparse attention; this is the weight-quantization version. None of D1-D4.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict different positions (high-entropy routing moves length, low-entropy routing moves accuracy), as the card's expert does. The 'slipped digit triggers re-checking' story and the -0.73 length-accuracy correlation give real doubt.
reasons.generative: A gives a 4-bit decoder with full-precision re-scoring on a narrow token class sharing the KV cache; B collapses to a serving configuration (4-bit plus a marker penalty), which is a settings recommendation.
reasons.reviewer: Token-level routing for quantized reasoning models is already crowded (ReQAT, DMR, and RATIO 2609.39801 found in query 4 on token-level optimisation for quantized reasoning). The design keeps a full-precision model in memory, which undercuts the point of quantizing.
reasons.feasible: Two 4B copies fit on one card and a per-token logit-switch loop is easy to write. It runs outside vLLM at lower throughput, and 150 problems may be too few to separate arms when the INT4 length effect is small.

ranked.question: In a hybrid of recurrent (Gated DeltaNet) and attention layers, what decides which depth can be removed: the layer type or the position in the stack, and is there less removable depth than in a dense model of the same family?

evidence.claim: The early-exit study says state-space and hybrid models have less spare depth than dense transformers, gives an untested reason, and has no numeric comparison in the text.
evidence.source: arXiv 2603.23701, The Diminishing Returns of Early-Exit Decoding in Modern LLMs (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "dense transformers generally offer greater early-exit potential than Mixture-of-Experts and State Space Models."; "SSM further minimize redundancy by tightly coupling sequential state updates across depth."

evidence.claim: A layer-ablation study says the opposite about tolerance to random layer removal, but only on sub-1B models, without healing, and at damage levels where both models are already broken.
evidence.source: arXiv 2603.22473, Component Ablation for Efficient Hybrid Language Model Architectures (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: the hybrid has "greater normalized tolerance to matched random layer removal than the same-family Transformer control."; Qwen3.5-0.8B: "removing linear attention increases perplexity from 7.6 to 268,337", removing attention gives 625.

evidence.claim: The ablation study's explanation for the hybrid's tolerance is a hypothesis the authors say needs validating.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the surviving component type in neighboring layers partially compensates for structural disruption, but this mechanism should be validated in additional model families."

evidence.claim: Layer-importance structure is reported to differ between transformers and Mamba-style state-space models, which bears on whether healing after pruning behaves the same way.
evidence.source: arXiv 2609.16537, What Does Layer-Importance Reveal About Transformers and State-Space Models? (abstract)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Necessity and Plasticity anti-align across depth, whereas in the evaluated Mamba-style SSMs they point to overlapping regions."

evidence.claim: By a residual-stream similarity measure, Qwen3.5 sits in the same correlated-updates regime as dense models, which argues for similar spare depth.
evidence.source: arXiv 2609.31098, The Residual Stream's Effective Depth (abstract)

evidence.claim: The user's own depth-pruned hybrid-family models failed after quantization; whether architecture, missing healing or AWQ caused it is not separated.
evidence.quote_or_number: "All depth-pruned AWQ variants: IFEval 0.05–0.20"

ranked.expert_prediction: Position decides: late-middle blocks are removable whatever their type, early blocks are not, and a hybrid has about as much removable depth as a dense model of the same size.
ranked.why_uncertain: The two papers that compare architectures disagree and both are weak (one has no numbers in the text, the other compares broken models under 1B). A removed recurrent layer also removes a state that later tokens read, so the damage could grow with sequence position in a way a removed attention layer's does not, and nobody has measured that at a useful operating point (10-25% of layers, models of 4B and up).
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: "layer pruning OR layer skipping hybrid Gated DeltaNet OR Mamba attention LLM which layers removable Qwen3.5 depth redundancy linear attention layers versus attention layers 2026". Semantic Scholar citations of 2609.16537 (none) and 2603.23701 (two, unrelated to hybrids).
ranked.closest_existing_answer: arXiv 2603.22473 (component ablation on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Falcon-H1-0.5B: removes all layers of a type or single components, no healing, sub-1B only).
ranked.outcome_a: Type matters. If attention layers are the cheap ones to remove, removal also deletes their KV cache, so it is a memory saving as well as a compute saving; if recurrent layers are, compute drops and the cache is untouched. Either way one builds a type-aware selection rule, and if hybrids turn out to have clearly less removable depth, depth methods are dropped for this model family in favour of bit-width.
ranked.outcome_b: Position only, same as dense. Then contiguous-block removal with repair carries over unchanged, and the user's collapse is a healing or calibration problem, not an architecture problem.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A layer-removal or layer-skip rule for GDN hybrids such as Qwen3.5, or a decision not to pursue depth reduction in that family.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B against Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. Single-block bypass sweep with teacher-forced KL on 256 reasoning traces of about 2k tokens, split by layer type and position, and reported as a function of token position (does bypassing a recurrent layer hurt more late in the sequence). Then contiguous-block removal of 2 to 8 blocks with a linear repair, scored on KL and on GSM8K and IFEval. Stop if the hybrid's bypass-KL profile over depth overlays the dense model's and layer type explains under 10% of the variance once position is accounted for: nothing hybrid-specific to build.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near residue (b) and earlier questions on hybrids only in subject (hybrid models); it is about removable depth, not attention diffuseness or state checkpoints (D2). Shape is close to "does X hold in hybrids", so this is the weakest card.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict position mostly decides, with attention layers in the hybrid less removable because there are only a few; that differs from the card's expert, which is a sign of some split. Still close to a 'does X hold in hybrids' question with a guessable main effect.
reasons.generative: Only the type-matters branch yields a selection rule, and it may instead yield 'drop depth methods for hybrids'; the position-only branch says existing methods carry over unchanged. Self-described as the weakest card.
reasons.reviewer: Shape is 'does depth pruning behave the same in hybrids', with position-decides the likely answer. The card itself rates it weakest; only the token-position growth of recurrent-layer bypass damage is new.
reasons.feasible: A single-block bypass sweep with teacher-forced KL on 4-9B models and a linear repair for contiguous removal is about one GPU-day of forward passes. The only requirement is a PyTorch path for the Qwen3.5 recurrent layers.

ranked.question: Do depth removal (layer skipping or depth pruning) and 4-bit weights get the same tokens wrong, or different ones?

evidence.claim: At item level, flips from structural compression and flips from low-bit quantization are predicted by different properties of the intact model: structural flips by a mid-depth dip, quantization flips by final margin.
evidence.source: arXiv 2607.04640, Wrong Before Right: Late Rescue and Interface Failure in Aligned Language Models (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "items with large dips on the intact model are 3–7×more likely to flip under genuine late-layer low-rank compression, block dropping, or structured pruning"; "deaths under 3-bit RTN quantization are dip-blind (item-level ρ≈0 in all four models)"

evidence.claim: At task level, a different paper finds one shared order of failure across pruning, quantization and random damage within a model, measured on short answers only.
evidence.source: arXiv 2611.11695, Language model capabilities fail in a shared, predictable order under compression and perturbation (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "task effects under Wanda, SparseGPT and GPTQ correlate with the same model's random-damage task effects with a median of 0.875 over 18 cells."; "Generation used at most 32 new tokens"

evidence.claim: Draft acceptance under greedy verification is set by total variation for every compression family tested, including layer removal, but which positions flip, whether families overlap, and what happens when two are stacked were not studied.
evidence.source: arXiv 2610.00694, How Divergence Becomes Decision Flips in Compressed Language Models (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: flip rate "tracks total variation at a ratio with median 1.05, with no fitted constant."; "Total variation predicted greedy acceptance with mean errors of 1.1–2.4% and ranked the drafts at Spearman 0.86–1.00."; "Every statistic is measured under teacher forcing on greedy references."

evidence.claim: Quantization divergence concentrates where the full-precision model is itself uncertain.
evidence.source: arXiv 2606.00206, Quantized Reasoning Models Think They Need to Think Longer, but They Do Not (full text)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Position-level KL divergence correlates strongly with the BF16 model's next-token entropy (Spearman ρ=0.92)."

evidence.claim: The sparse-attention self-draft reports high acceptance but compares only against n-gram and EAGLE3 drafts; combining it with other approximations is discussed, not measured.
evidence.quote_or_number: "PillarAttn achieves an average acceptance token length of 6.16 out of 8 tokens"; "SparseSpec can be combined with other lightweight drafting methods, including EAGLE3 and MTP"

ranked.expert_prediction: Partial overlap, well above chance, and most of it explained by one thing: both families fail where the full model's top-two margin is small. After conditioning on target entropy the remaining overlap is small.
ranked.why_uncertain: 2607.04640 finds a clean dissociation (quantization flips ignore the property that predicts structural flips), but on minimal pairs with single-token scoring. 2611.11695 finds a shared order, but at task level with 32-token outputs. Neither is token-level on generated reasoning text, and layer-skip errors could sit on confident tokens that need late layers (the late-rescue items), which entropy would not flag.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: "do quantized, layer-skipped, pruned and sparse-attention draft models make the same token errors? overlap of rejected tokens across draft types speculative decoding multiple drafts OR compound OR cascade self-speculative 2026". Semantic Scholar citations of 2607.04640 (one, unrelated) and 2610.00694 (none). Read 2611.11695 and 2610.00694 in full for an overlap or stacking analysis: neither has one.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: arXiv 2607.04640 (dissociation at item level on minimal pairs; overlap of the flip sets is not reported) and arXiv 2611.11695 (shared order at task level).
ranked.outcome_a: Same tokens (errors are nested and tracked by one difficulty signal): approximations can be stacked in a single draft (layer skip plus 4-bit plus sparse attention) and acceptance stays near that of the worst member, so draft cost multiplies down while acceptance does not. One cheap gate (target margin) sets draft length for all of them.
ranked.outcome_b: Different tokens: a stacked draft loses acceptance roughly as the union of the error sets, so stacking is a poor trade. The useful design is per-token routing between two cheap drafts, or a cascade, with headroom equal to one minus the chance that both are wrong. The layer-skip errors on confident tokens would also be a direct measure of how much late-layer work a token needs.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Whether a self-speculative drafter should be one compound approximation or several alternative approximations with a router.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B (and Qwen3-4B as a check), teacher-forced on about 200 greedy full-precision reasoning traces from MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench (about 2M positions). Record the per-position top-1 mismatch for: bypass of 4 and 8 middle blocks, early exit at depth L-k through the final norm and head, 4-bit RTN / AWQ / GPTQ, and Qwen3-1.7B as an unrelated small draft. Tune each to roughly the same flip rate (about 10%). Report pairwise overlap against independence, overall and inside bins of full-model entropy, and the flip rate of the stacked variant (bypass plus 4-bit) against the union and the maximum of the two. Stop if, inside entropy bins, overlap is within 1.2x of independence for every pair and the full-model margin predicts both error sets equally well: then entropy is the whole story and there is no new gate to build.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: none of D1-D4. Two sibling harvests ask the same thing for a sparse-KV draft vs a 4-bit draft; this card is the depth-removal vs 4-bit version and rests on the 2607.04640 dissociation. Not in the earlier 35 questions.

reasons.unpredictable: Same shape as F06: partial overlap above chance, mostly explained by target margin, plus a modest set of confident-token layer-skip errors. The headline answer is predictable; only the size of the late-layer residual is open.
reasons.generative: A supports a compound draft with one margin gate and B a router or cascade, but the card's own stop condition (entropy explains everything) leaves no new gate, and the design is a duplicate of the sparse-KV versus W4 sibling with less kernel consequence.
reasons.reviewer: Third variant of the 'do two drafts fail at the same tokens' family, with 2607.04640 and 2611.11695 already close and entropy likely explaining most overlap. Layer-skip plus W4 drafts are not a strong design target.
reasons.feasible: Teacher-forced top-1 mismatch for block bypass, early exit, public 4-bit copies and a small model on 200 stored traces needs only standard PyTorch. About one GPU-day.

ranked.question: Is the KV subset that best preserves task accuracy when used alone also the one that gives the longest accepted runs when used as a draft, or are these two different objectives?

evidence.claim: VeriCache uses off-the-shelf compressors as drafts and says outright that draft quality is a different objective, untested.
evidence.quote_or_number: Existing compressors optimize direct-serving accuracy; a compressor designed to maximize acceptance length at large draft horizons—a different objective—could push VeriCache’s throughput further.

evidence.claim: A static 4x compaction with no refresh sustains long accepted runs: about 19-23 of 30 (per-token rate about 0.97-0.98 by my arithmetic), higher than refreshed 5% drafts.
evidence.quote_or_number: at draft length 30, VeriCache at 4× compaction sustains acceptance lengths of ∼19 on Qwen-32B and ∼23 on Llama-70B

evidence.claim: A ranking inversion: SnapKV, normally the better stand-alone compressor, falls below a plain recent-window cache as a draft at longer draft length.
evidence.quote_or_number: When forced to a longer horizon (k=10), its acceptance rate degrades below that of StreamingLLM due to permanent information loss.

evidence.claim: For MLA-converted drafts, errors that do not hurt stand-alone generation do hurt acceptance.
evidence.quote_or_number: attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance

evidence.claim: Attention that is best for predicting the next token is not the best guide to which pages matter.
evidence.quote_or_number: attention at the last layer is specialized for next-token prediction and less representative of overall page importance

evidence.claim: As stand-alone caches on a needle task, StreamingLLM and H2O fail, while as drafts on ordinary text they exceed 90% acceptance with 1K entries.
evidence.quote_or_number: practical implementations like H2O and StreamingLLM exhibit promising results, achieving over 90.5% acceptance rates with 1K KV cache budget ... There is a notable drop in StreamingLLM and H2O’s results on needle retrieval.

evidence.claim: The lossy-compression side reports failures that average token agreement would not show.
evidence.source: VeriCache, arXiv 2605.17613 (abstract, read earlier in session)
evidence.quote_or_number: catastrophic failures in code generation and tool calling

ranked.expert_prediction: The two rankings mostly agree, since both measure closeness to dense output, with one exception: recency-heavy selections do better as drafts than their stand-alone accuracy suggests.
ranked.why_uncertain: Acceptance is an average over all tokens and is dominated by easy, locally determined ones; task accuracy hangs on a few answer-bearing tokens. The SnapKV versus StreamingLLM inversion and the MLA result both show the two can separate, and VeriCache's static, query-agnostic compaction reaching longer runs than refreshed top-K drafts does not fit SparseSpec's premise that the needed entries shift during generation. The reverse failure is also possible: a selector with high acceptance that is useless alone.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: 'KV cache' + compression + acceptance + draft (RIFT 2610.31098, 2608.30252, 2607.27269, 2604.26412); 'speculative decoding' + KV + (eviction OR SnapKV OR H2O) (Dustin, SpecExtend 2505.20776, a survey); 'speculative decoding' + ('sparse attention' OR 'sparse KV') (20 hits checked). Read VeriCache 4.3 and discussion, MagicDec 4.4, SparseSpec-L sensitivity section.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: MagicDec (2408.11049) compares SnapKV and PQCache as drafts by acceptance and cost but not against their stand-alone accuracy. RIFT (2610.31098) and BudgetDraft (2606.00144) train drafts for compressibility, which assumes the objectives differ without measuring it. Beyond KV Reconstruction (2607.27269) shows the gap for MLA conversion, not for KV selection.
ranked.outcome_a: Rankings agree: the KV-compression literature's best selectors can be used as drafts unchanged, and per-token acceptance against dense, which needs one replay pass, becomes a cheap offline proxy for compression quality in place of full benchmark runs.
ranked.outcome_b: Rankings disagree: a draft needs a different selection objective (keep what makes the next k tokens match, mostly recent and verification-guided entries) from a stand-alone cache (keep what the final answer depends on). Acceptance is then not a valid proxy for compression quality, and a combined system should hold two populations of KV: a small draft set and a separately chosen retained set.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either 'acceptance as the evaluation metric for KV compression' (a tool) or a draft-specific selection objective with a two-population cache. It also says whether VeriCache-style systems should design their own compressor.
ranked.first_experiment: Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Selectors: recent window (StreamingLLM), H2O, SnapKV, previous-step top-K (PillarAttn-style), oracle top-K, and KVzip if its code runs; budgets 5, 10, 25%. For each selector x budget cell measure (i) stand-alone accuracy when the model decodes with only that subset, on a LongBench subset, RULER needle and QA, and 200 MATH-500 problems with reasoning; (ii) per-token acceptance and mean accepted run at k=8 and k=30 against dense on the same items, by teacher-forced replay. Report Kendall tau between the two rankings per task. Decide A if tau >= 0.8 on all tasks; decide B if at least one selector pair inverts with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs on two or more tasks. Stop if all selectors are within noise of each other on stand-alone accuracy at these budgets (no ranking to compare).
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Touches D1 (KV selection at decode time) in that selectors are compared, but asks a different thing: whether two published uses of the same selectors optimise the same property. No engine or page-fetch measurement. Not related to D2-D4.

reasons.unpredictable: I would confidently predict the rankings diverge on needle/long-prompt tasks: a recency window gets high per-token acceptance but fails retrieval, while SnapKV does the opposite. The SnapKV/StreamingLLM inversion already in print essentially gives the answer.
reasons.generative: B gives a draft-specific selection objective and a two-population cache, which is a real design; A yields only an evaluation proxy (acceptance as a metric) and 'use existing selectors unchanged'.
reasons.reviewer: Whether compression-accuracy and draft-acceptance rankings agree is untested and has a tool-or-design payoff. The expected answer (mostly agree, recency exception) limits surprise, and it is a broad benchmark sweep that reviewers treat as incremental.
reasons.feasible: Stand-alone accuracy needs six selectors (including closed-loop oracle top-K and KVzip) in one decoding harness across three budgets, three task families and two models, on top of the acceptance replay. That is a multi-week integration, and a Kendall tau over six selectors has little power.

ranked.question: Does low-bit value-cache damage come from the bias of the rounding rather than its size, as reported for recurrent state, while key damage comes from variance?
ranked.tension_type: paper A's explanation predicts P, paper B's data shows not-P

evidence.claim: For cached recurrent state, same-width unbiased rounding removes the damage.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Same-width bf16 SR removes the length increase in four of five affected models ... so the failure is mostly rounding bias, not missing resolution."

evidence.claim: For keys, an unbiased estimator is worse because softmax amplifies its variance.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Although QJL debiases the inner product estimations, we found that its variance is amplified by Softmax, thus degrading both attention quality and downstream accuracy."

evidence.claim: The MSE-optimal quantizer is biased, yet removing a rank-1 component beats spending a bit on debiasing.
evidence.quote_or_number: "the Lloyd-Max quantizer systematically shrinks each coordinate toward zero"; "Even a simple rank-1 SVD at 2.04 bits matches standalone TQprod at 3.00 bits"

evidence.claim: Values tolerate 2 bits on perplexity but not on arithmetic and knowledge tasks.
evidence.quote_or_number: KVTuner, Llama3-8B-Instruct: KV8 9.95 vs K8V2 10.04. KVTC: "stronger compression of values shows a noticeable degradation on the GSM8K and MMLU tasks"

evidence.claim: A second-order argument says deterministic and zero-mean perturbations of the same size cost different amounts; no experiment at matched storage.
evidence.quote_or_number: "a deterministic perturbation a u has quadratic cost a^2 u^T G u/2. Idealized zero-mean uniform rounding noise of width Delta has expected quadratic cost Delta^2 u^T G u/24 ... It is not a universal bound or a matched-total-storage comparison."

ranked.expert_prediction: For values, bias matters more than size in diffuse heads, because attention averages out zero-mean noise across the tokens it reads. For keys, variance matters and the MSE-optimal quantizer is the right one.
ranked.why_uncertain: A KV entry is written once and its error is frozen, so unbiased rounding can only help across tokens inside one attention read, not across decoding steps. Recurrent state is rewritten every step, so its bias accumulates; the recurrent result may simply not transfer. The two KV data points that exist (LowRAM, eOptShrinkQ) both say debiasing does not help, but both concern inner products on the key side.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv API: all:"KV cache" AND ("stochastic rounding" OR dither OR "unbiased quantization" OR "error coherence" OR "coherent error") returned 2611.01864, a quantized JL paper, WitCert 2607.28699, DASHQuant; none compares biased and unbiased rounding for keys and values separately. WebSearch on bias, variance and stochastic rounding in KV quantization found no such analysis.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: Lost in Rounding (2611.12127) answers it for recurrent state only. LowRAM's QJL note and eOptShrinkQ's TQprod comparison cover unbiased inner products for keys. WitCert (2607.28699, abstract) uses a subtractively dithered INT8 quantizer for certification, not to test the effect.
ranked.outcome_a: Bias dominates for values: choose the quantizer family by tensor, not only the bit width. Unbiased or dithered rounding for values, MSE-optimal for keys, and fewer value bits in diffuse heads.
ranked.outcome_b: Error size dominates: MSE-optimal everywhere, and the bias effect is specific to state that is rewritten each step. In a hybrid model the attention cache and the recurrent state then need different quantizers.
ranked.design_it_points_to: An asymmetric choice of quantizer family for keys, values and (in hybrids) recurrent state.
ranked.first_experiment: Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-9B. Quantize values, then keys, at 2 and 3 bits with nearest rounding, stochastic rounding on the same grid, Lloyd-Max, and Lloyd-Max with the shrink rescaled away. Per head, split attention-output error into mean and variance terms; measure teacher-forced next-token KL; then run closed loop on 200 GSM8K / MATH-500 problems for accuracy and generated length. Stop if nearest and stochastic rounding differ by under 5% in KL and within noise in accuracy for both tensors.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near earlier residue (a) (one offline predictor of reasoning-length inflation) and earlier Q25 (decode-phase quantization error accumulation). It differs by asking which part of the error does the damage for each tensor, with length as one readout rather than the target.

reasons.unpredictable: KV entries are written once, so there is no step-to-step accumulation for bias to exploit; I would predict MSE size dominates and stochastic rounding is no better or worse at 2-3 bits. The two existing KV data points (LowRAM, eOptShrinkQ) already say debiasing does not help.
reasons.generative: Both outcomes are a choice of quantizer family per tensor (dithered versus MSE-optimal), which is a settings recommendation over existing quantizers rather than a new method.
reasons.reviewer: Weak premise: KV entries are written once, nearest-rounding error is already roughly zero-mean across tokens, and both existing data points say debiasing does not help. Likely outcome is 'MSE-optimal everywhere', which changes nothing.
reasons.feasible: Quantize-dequantize hooks at K/V write time give both the teacher-forced KL and closed-loop generation without kernel work. Four rounding schemes on 200 problems across three 8-9B models is a couple of GPU-days.

ranked.question: When the decode kernel reads low-bit (INT4/INT2) KV, do dequantisation and multi-token speculative verification draw on the same spare instruction-issue budget per KV byte, so that their speedups stop multiplying, and is it the GPU or the kernel template that decides where that happens?

evidence.claim: Speculative verification is said to be cheap because compute sits idle while KV is loaded.
evidence.quote_or_number: The high ratio of peak FLOPS to memory bandwidth in modern GPUs causes the increase in KV loading time with batch size to outweigh the increase in computation time (see Fig. 1). As a result, although compute-bound linear layers increase verification cost, it is mitigated by the KV bottleneck.

evidence.claim: Same framing in a 2026 paper: speculative decoding helps by raising arithmetic intensity.
evidence.quote_or_number: speculative decoding ... mitigates the bandwidth bottleneck by increasing arithmetic intensity, while sparse attention ... directly reduces the volume of accessed KV cache.

evidence.claim: Low-bit KV kernels are limited by instruction issue, not bandwidth, and the spare budget is small on H100 and gone on B200.
evidence.quote_or_number: reconstruction alone can consume 30% and 60% of H100's peak hardware budget of 9.99 lane-slots/byte ... At peak HBM throughput, INT2 reconstruction exceeds B200's hardware peak of 4.65 lane-slots/byte, and INT4 reconstruction alone consumes 86% of that peak.

evidence.claim: The gap widens with newer cards.
evidence.quote_or_number: From H100 to B200, peak HBM throughput grows 2.39x, while peak instruction-issue throughput grows only 11%

evidence.claim: FOSCAR is evaluated for single-token decode at batch 1, 8 and 64; I found no multi-row (verification) measurement in the sections I read.
evidence.quote_or_number: batch 1, 8, 64 (single-query decode); H100 INT2/INT4 3.36x/2.83x over FlashInfer BF16; B200 2.67x/2.30x

evidence.claim: On a bandwidth-poor consumer card, low-bit decode reaches close to the ideal byte ratio.
evidence.quote_or_number: Results on Bandwidth-constrained GPU (RTX 4090) ... BitDecoding achieves roughly 4x (4-bit) and over 7x (2-bit) speedups over FlashDecoding-v2

evidence.claim: The standard decode kernel uses a CUDA-core template for one query row and tensor cores only from 16 rows, so the instruction demand of a 2-9 row verification depends on which template is picked.
evidence.quote_or_number: For query tile size 1, we use CUDA Cores template since tensor core instruction m (minimum rows) is 16, and use Tensor Cores for other query tile sizes

evidence.claim: On the user's RTX 6000 Ada the clock that sets the issue budget moves by more than 2x with the kernel mix.
evidence.quote_or_number: a memory-bound kernel holds 2.67 GHz while cuBLAS SGEMM runs at 1.19 GHz

evidence.claim: On the user's Ada, fp8 KV already gives less than the 0.5 byte ratio at the step level.
evidence.quote_or_number: fp8 KV step-time ratio 0.70 at 32K x 16, 0.79 at 8K x 64

ranked.expert_prediction: On RTX 6000 Ada the two gains multiply: the card has roughly 21 to 52 lane-slots per byte (my estimate: 142 SMs x 128 lane-slots x 1.1 to 2.67 GHz / 926 GB/s), four to eleven times B200's 4.65, so INT4 or INT2 dequantisation plus 8-token verification both fit. On H100 they partly compete and on B200 low-bit KV leaves no room for verification rows, so there the gains do not multiply.
ranked.why_uncertain: The demand side is not known. Dequantisation cost is per KV byte, but verification adds a per (query row, token) cost for the softmax exponent that runs on CUDA cores, and the QK/PV product costs about ten times more issue slots on the CUDA-core template than on tensor cores (my estimate: about 4600 vs 300 to 550 lane-slots per KV-head token for 36 rows). With GQA group 4 and 9 verified tokens the 36 rows per KV head sit between the two templates. Also the Ada clock drops to about 1.1 GHz when GEMMs share the step, which cuts the issue budget by 2.4x, so INT2 with k=8 could be marginal even on Ada. Either direction is defensible from the published numbers.
ranked.prior_answer_search: WebSearch: 'speculative decoding quantized KV cache verification compute bound low-bit attention kernel'; 'multi-token verification attention kernel INT4 2-bit KV cache instruction throughput'. Semantic Scholar keyword queries 'speculative decoding quantized KV cache verification' and 'QuantSpec self-speculative decoding hierarchical quantized KV cache' were rate-limited and returned nothing. Read FOSCAR, BitDecoding, SSV, MagicDec, SparseSpec; abstracts of QuantSpec 2502.10424, Quasar 2603.01399.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: FOSCAR (2611.09722) gives the issue-budget model but only for single-row decode. QuantSpec (2502.10424) drafts with a 4-bit KV cache but the verifier reads full-precision KV and there is no kernel-level budget analysis. Quasar (2603.01399) quantises verifier weights, not KV. None measures verification width over a low-bit KV kernel.
ranked.outcome_a: The gains multiply on Ada-class cards (bandwidth-poor, issue-rich): then quantised KV plus self-speculation is the right stack for 48 GB GDDR6 cards, the ranking of methods differs from the HBM ranking in the papers, and one builds a verification kernel over INT4/INT2 KV and reports the per-card budget as the predictor.
ranked.outcome_b: They compete even on Ada (or only on the CUDA-core template): then the usable draft length k is a function of KV bit-width and card, and one builds either a verification kernel that dequantises a KV tile once and feeds 16-row tensor-core MMA, or a scheduler that picks (bit-width, k) jointly from a two-term budget model.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A joint (KV bit-width, verification width, kernel template) rule expressed in lane-slots per byte, and a fused low-bit verification kernel if the budget is tight.
ranked.first_experiment: Kernel microbenchmark on one RTX 6000 Ada, no model needed: synthetic KV at Llama-3.1-8B / Qwen3-8B shapes (Hkv=8, G=4, D=128), context 8K and 32K, batch 16 and 64. Run FlashInfer BF16 decode and the BitDecoding INT4 and INT2 kernels with query rows per request q in {1, 2, 4, 9, 16}. Measure effective KV bytes/s as a fraction of 926 GB/s, and log the SM clock. Repeat with a GEMM running in between to force the 1.1 GHz clock. Fit demand = a (per byte) + b x q (per row-token pair) against the estimated budget. Stop if the bandwidth fraction for INT2 stays within 10% of its q=1 value up to q=16 under both clock conditions; then the answer on this hardware is 'they multiply' and only the cross-card model is left to write down.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: none. It uses the SparseSpec background (verification cost) and is not D1 to D4. It is not a 'does gain G survive C' question because the two papers' models give opposite predictions depending on a quantity nobody has measured.

reasons.unpredictable: The card's own budget estimate gives Ada 4-11x the issue budget per byte of B200, and even after the 2.4x clock drop it stays above; first principles say the gains multiply on bandwidth-poor GDDR6 cards. Doubt only on the CUDA-core-template demand term.
reasons.generative: Both outcomes lead to a kernel: a verification kernel over INT4/INT2 KV if gains multiply, or a fused dequantise-once tensor-core verification kernel plus a joint (bit-width, k) scheduler if they compete. The risk is that on Ada the answer is just 'they multiply' and a budget number.
reasons.reviewer: A joint bit-width and verification-width budget model would interest a kernel/ASPLOS audience and no paper measures it. It rests on many self-made estimates, and the likely result on Ada (gains multiply) leaves nothing to build.
reasons.feasible: The public low-bit decode kernels are single-row, so the multi-row sweep needs new INT4/INT2 verification kernels in both templates first. The GPU half of the question (H100, B200) cannot be measured on Ada/A6000 cards.

ranked.question: For a sparse-KV self-drafter, what decides, head by head, whether choosing KV entries by attention score gives more accepted tokens than signal-free sampling (prompt + recent window + uniform random), and does a key-query statistic measured offline predict which heads need selection?

evidence.claim: Theory: uniform sampling of KV entries is near-optimal for attention approximation in the similarity range real models show.
evidence.source: Attention under Bounded Key-Query Similarity (arXiv 2610.35020, 26 Oct 2026)
evidence.quote_or_number: "the simple uniform sampling algorithm is nearly optimal for a typical range of parameters, supporting its surprising effectiveness on real datasets"; "the empirical (a, b) values for widely used models lie in or close to the uniform sampling regime"

evidence.claim: That regime was measured with clipped quantiles, the sink removed, and one head per layer, so the few strongly aligned pairs a sharp head relies on may have been clipped away.
evidence.source: arXiv 2610.35020, Figure 3 caption and Appendix F
evidence.quote_or_number: "endpoints a and b computed as 0.001 and 0.999 quantiles of cosine similarities distribution. Initial-token (attention sink) is excluded." Appendix F uses query head 0 / KV head 0 of layers 4, 8, 16, 24.

evidence.claim: Second theory paper: random sampling is the minimax-optimal query-agnostic compressor; knowing the future-query distribution gives a sharp separation.
evidence.source: The risk of KV cache compression (arXiv 2607.01520, Jul 2026)
evidence.quote_or_number: "Random sampling already provides a strong query-agnostic baseline, consistent with its minimax optimality."; "sharp separation between algorithms with and without access to the future-query distribution"

evidence.claim: Empirical: random per-head eviction matches the best scored evictor on reasoning tasks, but the metric is task accuracy, generation gets longer, and a once-stated fact is lost.
evidence.quote_or_number: "The selection signal, in other words, contributes almost nothing beyond uniform random selection."; "Random Attention never recovers a passcode announced 57 compression rounds before the question, while R-KV recovers it 84 % of the time"; "eviction generally lengthens generation relative to full attention"

evidence.claim: Sparse self-speculation is built on the opposite premise and reports no random-selection baseline.
evidence.quote_or_number: "instead of using a static sparsity pattern (e.g., sliding window attention), a dynamic sparse attention mechansim that adapts to the context dynamics is necessary to achieve a high acceptance rate"; "PillarAttn achieves an average acceptance token length of 6.16 out of 8 tokens" at sparsity 0.05; baselines are EAGLE-3, N-gram, Streaming

evidence.claim: For a small drafter, restricting attention to a recent window did not cost acceptance.
evidence.source: Quantize the Target, Quantize the Drafter (arXiv 2607.04244)
evidence.quote_or_number: "In our experiments, SWA often increases the mean acceptance length and reduces decoding latency, especially for long-context inputs."

evidence.claim: Uniform sampling of prefill KV is within about a point of SnapKV on LongBench-E averages but loses several points in the low-error regime.
evidence.quote_or_number: Table 1 averages: Uniform 48.76 vs SnapKV 48.77; Uniform 49.88 vs SnapKV 50.22. Table 5: TriviaQA at rate 0.8, Uniform 86.3 vs baseline 91.6.

ranked.expert_prediction: At SparseSpec's 5% budget, top-K from verification attention beats random sampling on acceptance by a clear margin, because a few retrieval heads carry the next token. At 25% budget the gap is small. Most heads can be switched to recency plus uniform sampling at no cost; a minority cannot.
ranked.why_uncertain: The direction at 5% is fairly safe. What is not known is the head split and whether any cheap statistic finds it. Two theory papers say the measured similarity range puts real models in the uniform regime, but that measurement clipped the top 0.1% of pairs and used one head per layer. Random Attention's parity is on task accuracy after the model re-derives what it lost; token agreement, which a drafter needs, was not measured. If the (a, b) statistic without clipping, or the predictability of the next queries from the last verified ones, does not separate the heads, the theory is not describing the operative quantity.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search: "speculative decoding" "random eviction"; "self-speculative" "uniform sampling" KV; "speculative decoding" "sparse attention" draft acceptance; "KV cache" eviction "per head" random; "speculative decoding" "KV cache" compression draft. WebSearch: sparse self-speculative draft acceptance random vs top-k ablation 2026. Keyword scan for random/uniform baselines in the bodies of SparseSpec, Vegas (2602.07223), SparseSpec-L (2607.27735), ASPIRE (2609.17943), RIFT (2610.31098). None compares random or uniform selection with score-based selection on draft acceptance, and none tests the (a, b) regime per head.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: RIFT (2610.31098) compares attention-based, random and sliding-window masks, but for training a small drafter on long inputs, not for inference-time selection in a self-drafter ("the attention-based masking scheme outperforms every random and sliding-window control"). Protection Is (Nearly) All You Need (2605.18053) finds "scoring differences are secondary once boundaries are guarded", again on task F1.
ranked.outcome_a: Selection matters only in a small, identifiable set of heads, and an offline statistic finds them. Then a drafter reads a fixed strided or random subset for most heads and runs top-K only for the flagged ones: no refresh for most of the cache, contiguous reads, simpler kernels, and a principled per-head budget.
ranked.outcome_b: Selection matters in most heads, or no statistic separates them. Then the two theory papers and Random Attention describe task-level robustness, not next-token fidelity, and the bounded-similarity regime should not be used to design drafters. The useful output is the missing piece of theory: a bound stated for token agreement, with the queries of the last verified block as side information.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A per-head policy table computed once per model: uniform or strided KV for diffuse heads (with a log(1/p) logit bias so sampled entries stand in for the unsampled mass), verification-guided top-K only where the statistic says so. It also gives a rule for the refresh stride from query predictability.
ranked.first_experiment: Teacher-forced, no serving stack needed. Models: Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B (dense), Qwen3.5-9B (hybrid). Data: about 100 full-model reasoning traces (AIME, LiveCodeBench) of 8K to 16K tokens plus 50 long-input prompts. For draft blocks of k=8, compute accepted length under five KV policies at budgets 5%, 12.5%, 25%: (i) top-K from the previous verification's attention, per head; (ii) recent window only; (iii) prompt + recent + uniform random per head, with and without the log(1/p) bias; (iv) one shared strided draw; (v) top-K on a chosen head group, uniform elsewhere, sweeping the group. Per head record: (a, b) with and without quantile clipping, top-64 attention mass without the sink, and cosine between queries 8 steps apart. Stop if policy (iii) is at least one accepted token (of 8) below policy (i) at every budget and no per-head statistic predicts which head swaps are free better than AUC 0.65.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near D1 (decode-time KV page selection) and earlier questions Q32 and Q21. Differs: the setting is a lossless drafter where the cost of a bad selection is acceptance, not accuracy; the question is whether selection is needed at all per head and whether a theoretical regime statistic predicts it, not which selector is best.

reasons.unpredictable: Top-K beats random at 5% and a minority of retrieval-type heads carry it; a simple per-head statistic (entropy or top-64 mass) will very likely identify them. The card itself calls the direction safe; only the theory statistic's AUC is open.
reasons.generative: A gives a rich design (per-head policy table, strided reads for most heads, top-K only where flagged, refresh-stride rule) with kernel consequences; B says the theory does not apply and leaves a theory gap rather than something to build.
reasons.reviewer: Testing whether the bounded-similarity theory predicts per-head need for selection in a drafter is a fair theory-versus-practice check with a kernel-simplifying payoff. The direction at 5% budget is predictable and it overlaps D1 and the earlier Q21/Q32.
reasons.feasible: Policy (i) versus (iii) is reachable in about a week. The decisive part is per-head policies with a head-group sweep over hundreds of heads, k=8 draft blocks, three budgets and three models including a hybrid; that is a multi-week build and compute load.

ranked.question: Is the thinking a model produces after its answer has formed easier or harder for a draft to predict than the derivation before it, and does the answer differ between small independent drafts and sparse-attention self-drafts?

evidence.claim: Entropy is higher after commitment than before in thinking-mode models, and lower in no-think mode; the paper does not explain the difference.
evidence.quote_or_number: post-commitment entropy about 1.38-1.44x the pre-commitment value for Think models; falls for NoThink models

evidence.claim: Acceptance for independent drafts is slightly higher in the second half of the trace; the paper splits by position and token type, not by reasoning phase, and uses one target model.
evidence.source: Speculative Acceptance Does Not Decay with Position (arXiv 2610.30644)
evidence.quote_or_number: second half minus first half: +0.031 [+0.026, +0.036] same-family greedy, +0.069 [+0.063, +0.076] cross-family greedy; reflection tokens accepted at 0.747 vs >=0.93 for number and operator tokens

evidence.claim: Sparse-attention self-drafts get long accepted runs on reasoning traces, with no breakdown by phase, and the tokens they need change over the trace.
evidence.quote_or_number: "average acceptance token length of 6.16 out of 8 tokens"; "the critical tokens of the KV-Cache differs dramatically over time"

evidence.claim: Hedging words, where drafts fail, occur at similar rates before and after the commitment boundary.
evidence.quote_or_number: hedging words ("wait," "but") appear at similar rates before and after the boundary

evidence.claim: Concise training removes mostly post-answer tokens, so whatever the tail's draftability is, concise models change the mix.
evidence.quote_or_number: "86% [83, 90] of the thinking tokens it saves come after the answer has formed"

evidence.claim: An exit method built on a speculative-decoding head cut latency by less than it cut tokens; the paper gives no acceptance by phase.
evidence.quote_or_number: Qwen GSM8K: tokens -54%, latency 140.3 -> 75.8 (-46%)

ranked.expert_prediction: The tail is slightly easier for independent drafts (a few points of acceptance) and about the same for sparse self-drafts, so early exit and speculative decoding multiply almost cleanly.
ranked.why_uncertain: The entropy measurement on Qwen3 points the other way from the acceptance measurement on R1-Distill-Qwen-7B. Position is not phase: the answer forms anywhere from 13% to 75% of the trace depending on the model. For sparse self-drafts acceptance depends on how far back attention reaches, and a verification pass that re-reads the derivation could fall outside the selected tokens. Nobody has measured it for sparse or n-gram drafts.

ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2610.30644: acceptance by position for two independent drafts on one target. It weakens this card for independent drafts; it has no phase split, no entropy by position and no self-speculation.
ranked.outcome_a: Tail easier: speculative decoding and exit or concise training claim partly the same tokens, so combined speedups are less than the product and draft speedups should be re-measured on concise models. A phase-aware draft length (longer drafts after the answer forms) becomes worthwhile.
ranked.outcome_b: Tail harder, at least for sparse self-drafts: the tail costs more wall time per token than the derivation, so exit saves more time than its token share suggests, and a sparse draft should change its token selection when the answer forms (include the derivation, or stop drafting).
ranked.design_it_points_to: Phase-aware drafting (draft length or sparse-token selection switched at answer formation), and a rule for whether exit and drafting speedups multiply.

Teacher-force each trace and record per token: target entropy; probability the draft token matches for (i) a small independent draft (Qwen3-1.7B or R1-Distill-1.5B), (ii) a sparse-attention self-draft emulated with attention masks at SparseSpec's sparsity, (iii) an n-gram copy draft; plus attention distance. Compare before and after answer formation with within-trace paired tests. Stop if expected accepted length differs by under 5% between phases for all three drafts.

reasons.generative: The best case is a phase-switched draft length or selection, a small tweak with a predicted effect of a few points; the other branch is a multiplication rule for combining speedups, i.e. a number.
reasons.reviewer: 2610.30644 already answers the positional version for independent drafts and the expected effect is small. Only the sparse self-draft phase split is new, which is a table in another paper.

ranked.question: When two lossy techniques are stacked (weight quantization, KV quantization, KV eviction), do their per-token logit perturbations add, and do they point in the same direction?

evidence.claim: Composition is claimed as a multiplied saving without a measurement of interaction.
evidence.quote_or_number: "composes with GQA and quantization for up to 16× combined key cache compression"

evidence.claim: "Orthogonal" is asserted for quantized verification and drafting.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Being orthogonal to existing drafting strategies, Quasar offers a generic and efficient pathway to accelerate the verification leg of speculative execution."

evidence.claim: "Orthogonal axes" asserted for two lossy relaxations in SD.
evidence.quote_or_number: "The two adaptations operate on orthogonal axes and compound in effect."

evidence.claim: For one pair of weight-side techniques, orthogonality has been shown false.
evidence.source: Break Through the Compression Bottleneck (arXiv 2607.20434), abstract
evidence.quote_or_number: "This paper provides the first mathematical proof that low-rank decomposition and quantization are non-orthogonal."; "their combination leads to significant performance degradation"

evidence.claim: A measured conflict between two techniques that were expected to stack.
evidence.quote_or_number: "EAGLE-2 provides limited benefit for 4-bit weight quantized models (W4A16 and W4A8), indicating a potential conflict."

evidence.claim: Eviction and quantization of the KV cache each produce steady per-step divergence, so their sum is a meaningful quantity to test.
evidence.quote_or_number: "grows roughly linearly in t under KVzip 4× (left) and TurboQuant k4v3 (right)"

ranked.expert_prediction: At mild settings the perturbations add in logit space and their directions are unrelated, so KL adds. Their magnitudes are both largest at the same uncertain tokens. At aggressive settings the sum breaks down.
ranked.why_uncertain: If lossy techniques of different kinds all push probability toward the same small set of tokens (hesitation or restart words, as reported for weight quantization in 2606.00206, which I have not read), then directions align, KL grows faster than the sum, and the effect on reasoning length is superadditive even when each technique alone looks harmless. Whether eviction error has that same direction is unknown.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arXiv listing search: LLM compression "non-orthogonal" quantization; "pruning" "quantization" LLM "orthogonal" interaction "additive" error; "KV cache" quantization eviction "compose" error additive; LLM compression techniques combining order interference. Read the abstract of the one composition survey found (2607.20981, multimodal edge). No paper measures additivity or direction of output perturbations across technique families.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: 2607.20434 proves non-orthogonality for low-rank plus quantization applied to the same weight matrix, a different mechanism (both act on one tensor). 2607.20981 argues that techniques "cannot be treated as independent optimizations" for multimodal edge models, as a review, without a token-level test.
ranked.outcome_a: Perturbations add and directions are unrelated. Then "orthogonal" has a precise, checkable meaning, a stack's fidelity can be predicted from single-technique runs, and settings can be chosen per technique independently against one summed KL budget.
ranked.outcome_b: Directions align on a common set of tokens. Then stacks degrade faster than their parts, but one correction (a logit offset or calibration on that shared direction) would repair all of them at once, and budgets must be allocated jointly.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Either a cross-technique budget allocator that needs only single-technique measurements, or a shared output-side correction for stacked lossy inference.
ranked.first_experiment: Teacher-forced on 100 Qwen3-8B reasoning traces. Variants A = 4-bit weights, B = 4-bit KV, C = 4x eviction, and stacks AB, AC, BC, ABC. Per token, store centered logits over the full-model top-1000 tokens. Report: relative residual of delta_AB − delta_A − delta_B; cosine between delta_A and delta_B; KL_AB against KL_A + KL_B; the share of each delta that falls on a fixed list of hesitation tokens. Repeat at one more aggressive setting per technique. Stop if KL of every stack is within 10% of the sum and mean cosine is below 0.1 at both settings: the techniques are orthogonal in this sense and there is nothing to design.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Near residue (a) and earlier Q27 (early exit x quantization) and Q06/Q07. Differs: one-step, teacher-forced test of additivity and direction across families; no claim about a published gain surviving a condition.

reasons.unpredictable: At mild settings small perturbations linearise, so logit deltas add and KL is near-additive with a small positive cross term; this follows from first principles. The shared hesitation direction would at most give mild superadditivity, which most experts would also guess.
reasons.generative: B gives a shared output-side correction for stacked lossy inference, a real method; A gives a summed-KL budget allocator from single-technique runs, which is a settings procedure, and the card's stop condition is 'nothing to design'.
reasons.reviewer: Additivity and direction of stacked logit perturbations is teacher-forced only, and the expert answer (additive at mild settings) is probably right. The shared-direction correction is speculative and rests on an unread paper.
reasons.feasible: One-step teacher-forced logit deltas on 100 traces, using a public 4-bit copy, K/V quantization hooks and mask-emulated eviction, plus their stacks, is about one GPU-day. The additivity and cosine statistics are trivial.

ranked.question: Once the attention sink and softmax normalisation are removed, are the attention layers of a Gated DeltaNet hybrid in a different key-query similarity regime from the layers of a dense model, and does that regime, not the architecture label, decide which sparse-KV policy works?

evidence.claim: Local measurement: the hybrid's attention layers look about twice as diffuse, and the ranking of KV selectors flips.
evidence.source: Project log EXPERIMENTS.md entry H1, as quoted in the earlier question list
evidence.quote_or_number: "the oracle shared set at 512 misses 22.7% of attention on Qwen3.5-4B vs 11.6% on Qwen3-4B"; "Mean-key 25.5% beats Quest 31.8% on the hybrid; on dense mean-key is worst (19.5%) and Quest 14.3%"

evidence.claim: The earlier verification found a sink confound that could account for most of the gap but not for the ranking flip.
evidence.quote_or_number: "Renormalising the H1 miss rates over non-sink mass gives roughly 11.6/(1-0.408) = 19.6% for Qwen3-4B against 22.7/(1-0.034) = 23.5% for Qwen3.5-4B"; "This would not explain the selector ranking flip or the lookahead cost"

evidence.claim: Yet the hybrid cannot predict without its attention layers, so they are not doing dispensable averaging.
evidence.source: Component-Aware Self-Speculative Decoding in Hybrid Language Models (arXiv 2605.01106), abstract
evidence.quote_or_number: "Parallel hybrids achieve acceptance rates of alpha = 0.68 at draft length k=2 under greedy decoding, while sequential hybrids yield only alpha = 0.038"

evidence.claim: A sink-excluded, normalisation-free statistic now exists, with a theory saying what policy each regime wants; it has only been measured on dense 8B models.
evidence.source: Attention under Bounded Key-Query Similarity (arXiv 2610.35020), Figure 3
evidence.quote_or_number: "Empirical bounds a and b for 8B models Llama 3.1, Qwen3, and Ministral 3."; "Initial-token (attention sink) is excluded."

ranked.expert_prediction: Mostly an artifact: after sink renormalisation the hybrid and dense layers have similar concentration, and the hybrid's attention layers do sharp lookups as the mechanism papers say.
ranked.why_uncertain: The sink arithmetic does not explain why mean-key selection beats a query-aware selector on the hybrid only, or why one layer of lookahead costs far more there. Those two facts fit a model whose attention queries are hard to predict from earlier layers, which is a different property from diffuseness and would show up as a different (a, b) range or lower query predictability.
ranked.prior_answer_search: Relied on the earlier verification of Q23 (mechanism papers 2609.04434, 2611.01909, 2609.15545, 2606.15378 listed there; not reopened). New in this session: arXiv listing search for "speculative decoding" heterogeneous drafters (found 2605.01106) and reading 2610.35020. No paper reports the bounded-similarity statistic or a sink-free concentration measure for a hybrid model.
ranked.closest_existing_answer: The earlier verification's own back-of-envelope renormalisation (19.6% vs 23.5%), which is an inference from two published sink numbers measured on different prompts, not a measurement.
ranked.outcome_a: Same regime as dense once the sink is handled. Then hybrids need no special KV policy, the selector flip has another cause (query construction by the recurrent layers), and the work moves to query prediction across a GDN layer.
ranked.outcome_b: A different regime (wider similarity range or flatter mass). Then sparse-KV drafting and eviction budgets tuned on dense models do not transfer, and hybrids want sampling-style or mean-key policies; the (a, b) statistic becomes a quick per-model check before porting any KV method.
ranked.design_it_points_to: A per-model, per-head regime check that picks the KV policy for hybrid models, reusing the same table as the first card.
ranked.first_experiment: Step 1, no GPU: recompute the existing H1 miss rates over non-sink mass. Step 2: run Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-4B (then 9B and 8B) teacher-forced on the same 30 traces, so the text is identical, and record per head the unclipped and clipped (a, b), top-512 mass without the sink, and query cosine at lag 8. Stop if the renormalised gap is under 3 points and the per-head distributions of all three statistics overlap between the two models.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Heavy overlap with earlier Q23 and residue (b); adjacent to D2 only in that it concerns hybrid models (it is about their attention layers, not recurrent-state checkpoints). New: the bounded-similarity statistic as the normalisation-free measure, the same-text control, and 2605.01106 as counter-evidence. This is the weakest card and mainly a cross-architecture check of the first card's predictor.

reasons.unpredictable: The renormalisation (19.6% vs 23.5%) is already computed and I would predict the regimes overlap once the sink is removed, as the card's expert does. Only the explanation of the mean-key selector flip retains some doubt.
reasons.generative: The output is a per-model regime check (a statistic) and a confirmation or refutation of a normalisation artifact; outcome A moves the work elsewhere and outcome B says dense-tuned budgets do not transfer. Self-described as a cross-check of another card.
reasons.reviewer: Largely a restatement of residue (b) with a same-text control and a borrowed statistic. The card calls itself the weakest and the likely result (artifact) gives no design.
reasons.feasible: Step 1 is a recomputation on existing numbers with no GPU. Step 2 is per-head statistics on two 4B models over 30 traces, about half a GPU-day.

ranked.question: On a power-capped GPU, what sets the energy per floating-point operation of a matrix-multiply kernel: the tensor-core arithmetic, or the data movement around it?

evidence.claim: On the 300 W card the clock, not the cycle count, is what a dense kernel loses.
evidence.quote_or_number: "An RTX 6000 Ada starts a GEMM at its 2505 MHz boost bin, hits the power cap within ~15 ms, and settles near 1100 MHz."; "a memory-bound kernel holds 2.67 GHz while cuBLAS SGEMM runs at 1.19 GHz"

evidence.claim: Two kernels with a 2x difference in per-clock efficiency reach the same wall-clock throughput.
evidence.quote_or_number: 20_cublas bf16 107.55 TFLOP/s at 0.93 GHz, 79.5% SOL; 21_wmma bf16 109.39 TFLOP/s at 1.73 GHz, 43.6% SOL; "It is simply a cooler kernel, so the card lets it run 1.8x faster."

evidence.claim: The bare tensor-core instruction loop sustains about three times the throughput of cuBLAS at 2.5 times the clock, so the arithmetic alone does not hit the cap.
evidence.quote_or_number: bf16 mma m16n8k16: 343.8 burst, 329.3 sustained TFLOP/s at 2.34 SM GHz

evidence.claim: Published work covers the serving-level version only: compute-bound phases lose throughput with frequency, memory-bound decode does not.
evidence.quote_or_number: "compute-bound prefill loses throughput almost linearly with GPU frequency"; decode "sustains it down to 0.57x nominal"

evidence.claim: A decode-phase energy study on a 700 W card reports that power caps never bind during memory-bound decode.
evidence.source: The Illusion of Power Capping in LLM Decode, arXiv 2605.11999 (search snippet only)
evidence.quote_or_number: on an H200 the GPU draws 137-300 W during memory-bound decoding; clock locking recovers up to 32% of decode energy

ranked.expert_prediction: Data movement and control are most of the energy (the register-only loop shows that), but cuBLAS is already close to the minimum movement per operation, so a kernel can tie it and not beat it by more than about 10-20% sustained.
ranked.why_uncertain: The two own measurements pull apart. The tie between a 79.5% and a 43.6% per-clock kernel says energy per operation is nearly fixed regardless of kernel design. The 3x gap to the register-only loop says at least two thirds of GEMM energy is not arithmetic and is therefore in principle reducible. Nobody has attributed it.
ranked.prior_answer_search: arxiv.org listing 'LLM inference GPU power cap frequency throughput'; WebSearch 'GPU power cap clock frequency throttling GEMM tensor core energy per kernel efficiency LLM inference ...' (returned 2605.11999, 2608.21719, 2609.29707, 2501.08219, 2512.22066; all phase or serving level, none kernel level).
ranked.closest_existing_answer: PowerSlider (2608.21719) and 2605.11999 at phase level. No kernel-level energy attribution for tensor-core GEMM was found; older GPU power models were not searched.
ranked.outcome_a: Movement dominates and is reducible: on 300 W cards the sustained ceiling is set by bytes moved per operation. Tune kernels (or let an RL kernel search optimise) for sustained wall-clock in the power state the kernel itself induces; lower-precision weight formats then give more than their roofline gain in compute-bound phases because the clock rises.
ranked.outcome_b: Energy per operation is effectively fixed: there is no kernel-level headroom on capped cards. Serving on such cards should stay in memory-bound operating points, compute-bound prefill and large-batch verification are worth about 0.4x of their roofline value, and results from capped cards need clock-normalised reporting.
ranked.design_it_points_to: Energy-aware kernel search and power-state-aware benchmarking for workstation-class cards, or a serving policy that avoids compute-bound operating points on them.
ranked.first_experiment: RTX 6000 Ada, existing gemm-kernel harness. Sweep tile shape, register reuse, and staging path for bf16 and int8 mma kernels at 4096^3; log sustained TFLOP/s, SM clock and board power for each; fit energy per operation against bytes moved per operation. Then run vLLM prefill of a 27B fp8 model with clock logging to see whether the gap to the 193 TFLOP/s ceiling in the profiling notes is a clock gap. Stop if energy per operation varies by less than 10% across kernels that differ 2x in bytes moved.
ranked.dropped_direction_overlap: Close to D3 (single-GPU profiling for a bottleneck). Differs in that it asks what bounds a kernel under a power cap, from an unexplained result in the kernel project, and does not look for a vLLM bottleneck. Weakest fit of the five to the LLM-inference framing.

reasons.unpredictable: I would predict energy per operation is close to fixed across reasonable kernels and cuBLAS cannot be beaten by more than 10-20%; the register-only loop is cheaper simply because it does no loads. The measured tie between two very different kernels already points to this answer.
reasons.generative: A points at energy-aware kernel search but without a specified mechanism; B is a serving policy and a reporting convention for capped cards. The core output is an energy-per-operation attribution, i.e. a number.
reasons.reviewer: GEMM energy attribution on a power-capped card is outside what MLSys/NeurIPS/ICLR reviewers treat as LLM inference research, and it is close to killed D3. Not searched; either outcome yields a benchmarking caveat rather than an inference method.
reasons.feasible: Kernel variants, SM clock and board power logging on one Ada card with no model are reachable in a week for someone with kernel experience. Attribution rests on coarse board-level power from nvidia-smi, and it needs several kernels that differ 2x in bytes moved.
